explanation: Infections can irritate the bladder and cause sudden leaks. Ruling out an infection is always a smart first step in nursing assessment.

question: What is the common name for exercises designed to strengthen the pelvic floor muscles?

options.A: Aerobic exercises
options.B: Range of motion drills
options.C: Kegel exercises
options.D: Isometric stretches

explanation: Kegel exercises involve repeatedly contracting and relaxing the pelvic floor muscles to improve structural support and urinary control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: A patient with urge incontinence is starting a bladder retraining program. What is the right instruction to give them?

options.A: Stop doing pelvic floor exercises completely
options.B: Hold urine for as long as possible until severe pain occurs
options.C: Drink large amounts of water only right before bedtime
options.D: Urinate on a strict schedule, slowly increasing the time between trips

explanation: Bladder retraining uses a set schedule that slowly stretches out the time between bathroom breaks, helping the bladder hold more without sudden spasms.

question: Which type of medication is often given to calm down an overactive bladder?

options.A: Anticholinergics
options.B: Antibiotics
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Diuretics

explanation: Anticholinergic drugs block the nerve signals that tell the bladder muscle to squeeze too often. It helps the bladder relax!

question: What is the main goal of sling surgery done for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: To provide physical support under the urethra
options.B: To increase the total urine production rate
options.C: To shrink an enlarged prostate gland
options.D: To relax the overactive detrusor muscle

explanation: A sling creates a tiny hammock of mesh or tissue to lift and support the urethra so it stays shut when abdominal pressure spikes.

question: What is a very common skin problem caused by unmanaged urine leaks over time?

options.A: Incontinence-associated dermatitis
options.B: Chronic skin pigmentation loss
options.C: Diffuse bacterial cellulitis of the face
options.D: Severe subcutaneous fat necrosis

explanation: When urine sits on the skin, it breaks down the natural skin barrier, causing painful redness and irritation called incontinence-associated dermatitis.

question: Why does ongoing urinary incontinence put a patient at higher risk for urinary tract infections?

options.A: Skin breakdown allows bacteria to travel directly into the bloodstream
options.B: Frequent urination washes away all the normal protective cells
options.C: Moisture and residual urine create an environment where bacteria multiply easily
options.D: Absorbent pads permanently stop the kidneys from filtering waste

explanation: Sticking around in lingering moisture gives bacteria a cozy place to grow and easily find their way into the urinary tract. Good skin care and hygiene prevent this!

question: What main event causes urine to leak out in stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Complete blockage of the urethra
options.B: An overactive detrusor muscle spasm
options.C: A sudden urinary tract infection
options.D: Sudden physical pressure on the bladder

explanation: You've got this! Stress incontinence happens when sudden physical pressure—like coughing, laughing, or lifting—pushes urine out because the bladder pressure beats the urethra's grip.

question: Why do people often get confused by the word 'stress' in stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: They believe it is caused by mental exhaustion
options.B: They assume it only happens during high-intensity sports
options.C: They confuse it with neurological distress
options.D: They think it relates to emotional anxiety rather than physical pressure

explanation: It's an easy mix-up! In this case, 'stress' means physical force or pressure on your organs, not emotional stress or worry.

question: Which muscle group acts like a supportive hammock at the bottom of the pelvis?

options.A: Rectus abdominis muscles
options.B: Detrusor muscle group
options.C: Levator ani muscle group
options.D: Abdominal wall muscles

explanation: Think of the levator ani as a strong sling or hammock holding all your pelvic organs neatly in place. Great job!

question: What is the main job of the urethral sphincter in normal bladder control?

options.A: To sense when the bladder is completely full
options.B: To push urine out of the bladder during voiding
options.C: To stay contracted and maintain a tight seal against urine leakage
options.D: To stretch when the bladder fills with urine

explanation: The urethral sphincter acts like a tight valve, staying closed to keep urine inside until you're ready to use the bathroom.

question: What happens to the bladder and urethra during 'urethral hypermobility' when a patient coughs?

options.A: The bladder instantly shrinks in size
options.B: The urethral sphincter locks tightly shut to block flow
options.C: The detrusor muscle contracts with too much force
options.D: The bladder and urethra drop downward due to weak support

explanation: When the pelvic tissues are a bit weak, coughing causes the bladder and urethra to sag downward instead of staying firmly in place.

question: What does 'intrinsic sphincter deficiency' mean?

options.A: Blockage of urine flow by the prostate gland
options.B: Damage or weakness of the urethral sphincter muscle itself
options.C: A temporary infection lining the urinary tract
options.D: Overactivity of the main bladder muscle

explanation: Simply put, the valve muscle itself has lost some of its strength and can no longer seal tightly on its own.

question: A patient with long-term severe bronchitis has a higher risk for which type of urine leakage?

options.A: Overflow incontinence due to a blocked prostate
options.B: Stress incontinence due to repeated pressure from coughing
options.C: Urge incontinence due to bladder muscle irritation
options.D: Functional incontinence due to immobility

explanation: Constant coughing creates repeated downward pressure on the pelvic floor, which can wear down its support over time.

question: Which of these is NOT a common risk factor for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Obesity and excess body weight
options.B: Menopause and decreased estrogen levels
options.C: Frequent high-fluid intake throughout the day
options.D: Vaginal childbirth and multiple pregnancies

explanation: Drinking plenty of water is healthy! The real risk factors involve things that weaken pelvic support, like childbirth, hormonal shifts, or heavy pressure.

question: Why is a urinalysis always done when checking for stress incontinence?

options.A: To check kidney function and filtration rates
options.B: To measure the exact amount of residual urine left in the bladder
options.C: To test the patient for diabetes and high blood sugar levels
options.D: To rule out a urinary tract infection that can cause similar symptoms

explanation: Infections can mimic incontinence by irritating the bladder, so checking the urine first helps doctors make a clear diagnosis.

question: What is the purpose of a cough stress test during a physical checkup?

options.A: To check if coughing triggers a bladder spasm
options.B: To test the strength of the patient's respiratory muscles
options.C: To measure lung capacity while the patient lies flat
options.D: To observe if physical pressure causes immediate urine leakage

explanation: By asking the patient to cough, the clinician can watch directly to see if pressure causes any accidental leakage.

question: A nurse is teaching a patient how to do Kegel exercises correctly. What is the key instruction?

options.A: Contract the pelvic floor muscles as if trying to stop the flow of urine
options.B: Squeeze the abdominal and thigh muscles tightly while holding your breath
options.C: Push down gently as if having a bowel movement
options.D: Flex the buttocks and hips until your pelvis rises off the bed

explanation: Spot on! Kegels are all about squeezing those pelvic floor muscles—just like you're pausing your urine stream mid-flow, without squeezing your tummy or thighs.

question: Which lifestyle change helps the most in managing stress incontinence?

options.A: Drinking less than two cups of fluid per day
options.B: Achieving and maintaining a healthy body weight
options.C: Eliminating all forms of physical exercise completely
options.D: Increasing daily intake of carbonated beverages

explanation: Shedding extra pounds takes a huge amount of constant pressure off the pelvic floor muscles. You're doing great!

question: What is the main surgical option used to treat severe stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Widening the urethral opening with a stent
options.B: Placing a supportive sling under the urethra
options.C: Implanting an artificial kidney to filter urine
options.D: Removing the lower portion of the bladder

explanation: A surgical sling acts like a little hammock or seatbelt underneath the urethra to keep it from dropping when you move.

question: Why are pills and medications rarely the main treatment for stress incontinence?

options.A: Surgical options and pelvic therapy target the mechanical cause much more effectively
options.B: Medications for stress incontinence always cause permanent kidney damage
options.C: Pills are unable to dissolve inside the human digestive tract
options.D: Doctors prefer lifestyle changes because drugs are illegal for this use

explanation: Since stress incontinence is a physical, mechanical problem of loose support, fixing it requires physical strengthening or surgery rather than drugs.

question: What is a very common emotional or social challenge for patients with chronic stress incontinence?

options.A: False belief that they are pregnant
options.B: Uncontrolled aggressive behavior toward caregivers
options.C: Severe memory loss and cognitive decline
options.D: Social isolation and anxiety about public leaks

explanation: The fear of leaking in public can make patients feel embarrassed, causing them to stay home and miss out on social life.

question: Which skin problem happens most often when urinary incontinence is left untreated?

options.A: Deep pressure ulcers over the shoulder blades
options.B: Dry, scaly skin patches across the upper arms
options.C: Perineal dermatitis and breakdown from moisture
options.D: Fungal rashes spreading across the face and chest

explanation: When skin stays in contact with urine too long, the moisture breaks down the skin barrier and causes painful irritation or rashes.

question: What is the main job of a medical bougie?

options.A: To deliver high-flow oxygen therapy
options.B: To monitor internal body temperature
options.C: To navigate or explore narrow passages
options.D: To permanently remove tissue masses

explanation: Think of a bougie as a flexible guide. It's a slender tool used mainly to safely guide instruments or explore tight, narrow areas in the body.

question: How is a dilator different from a regular feeding tube?

options.A: A dilator is specifically designed to stretch tight strictures.
options.B: A dilator is only used for temporary fluid drainage.
options.C: A feeding tube contains a built-in cutting blade.
options.D: A feeding tube is rigid while dilators are always soft.

explanation: While feeding tubes are for giving food, dilators are specially sized and shaped to gently stretch out narrowed tubes in the body.

question: Which type of bougie uses heavy mercury or tungsten fillings so gravity helps it slide down?

options.A: Rigid urethral sounds
options.B: Eder-Puestow metal springs
options.C: Hurst or Maloney bougies
options.D: Pneumatic balloon dilators

explanation: Hurst and Maloney bougies have heavy tips filled with things like mercury or tungsten. This extra weight lets gravity help guide them smoothly down the esophagus.

question: When would a doctor choose a balloon dilator instead of a solid bougie?

options.A: When radial, controlled pressure is needed under direct visualization
options.B: When the patient is completely unconscious in the emergency room
options.C: When the stricture requires heavy metal weight to force it open
options.D: When direct tactile feedback through the hands is the only goal

explanation: Balloon dilators use air or fluid to expand outward evenly in all directions, and doctors usually place them using an endoscope so they can see what they're doing.

question: What is a very common cause of esophageal strictures (narrowing) that need dilation?

options.A: Chronic acid reflux disease
options.B: Benign gastric hypersecretion
options.C: Excessive dietary fiber intake
options.D: Congenital throat widening

explanation: When stomach acid keeps splashing up into the esophagus over a long time, it irritates the tissue, causes scarring, and makes the passage narrow.

question: A patient comes to the clinic struggling with a weak urine stream after a past pelvic injury. What procedure are they most likely getting ready for?

options.A: Gastric tube insertion
options.B: Urethral dilation
options.C: Endotracheal intubation
options.D: Esophageal manometry

explanation: Pelvic trauma can cause scarring in the urethra (the urine passage), leading to a tight spot or stricture that needs to be gently stretched out to restore normal flow.

question: Why is it important to check blood clotting lab results before a dilation procedure?

options.A: To assess the risk of bleeding from potential mucosal tears
options.B: To check if the patient has an active systemic infection
options.C: To calculate the exact dosage of local anesthetic required
options.D: To determine the correct size of the dilator to be used

explanation: Stretching tight tissues can sometimes cause minor scratches or tears. If a patient has poor blood clotting, those little tears could turn into heavy bleeding.

question: What is a key nursing duty right before an upper GI (throat and esophagus) dilation?

options.A: Administering a heavy oral laxative to clear the esophagus
options.B: Ensuring removable dental appliances are taken out
options.C: Instructing the patient to drink large volumes of water
options.D: Placing a heavy weighted blanket over the patient's chest

explanation: False teeth or removable dental plates can easily pop loose and block the airway during throat procedures, so they must always be taken out first.

question: During a sedated dilation procedure, what are the most critical vital signs for the nurse to keep watching?

options.A: Oxygen saturation and heart rate
options.B: Peripheral skin temperature
options.C: Capillary refill time
options.D: Bowel sound frequency

explanation: Because the patient is sedated and instruments are working near their airway or GI tract, monitoring their breathing (oxygen) and heart rate is top priority for safety.

question: Why does the nurse need to keep track of the exact sizes of the dilators used during the procedure?

options.A: To determine how long the patient must stay NPO afterward
options.B: To prevent the doctor from using metal instruments twice
options.C: To monitor the progressive widening of the stricture safely
options.D: To bill the hospital pharmacy for disposable plastic items

explanation: Doctors stretch the tissue step-by-step, going up in size very gradually. Tracking the sizes helps the team avoid jumping up in diameter too fast, which protects the patient from tearing.

question: What is the most serious and dangerous complication that can happen after a gastrointestinal dilation?

options.A: Mild throat irritation
options.B: Temporary hiccups
options.C: Visceral perforation
options.D: Dry mouth sensation

explanation: Perforation means a tear or hole gets poked through the wall of the esophagus or bowel. It's a medical emergency that happens if the tissue tears during stretching.

question: Which sign should immediately make a nurse suspect a post-procedure perforation after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: A slight drop in blood pressure after resting
options.B: Sudden severe chest pain and rising heart rate
options.C: Mild sore throat when swallowing saliva
options.D: Low-grade nausea from mild residual sedation

explanation: If a patient suddenly gets severe, worsening chest pain and a fast heart rate (tachycardia), it's a huge red flag that there might be a tear leaking into the chest cavity.

question: What warning signs should you teach a patient to report right away after going home from a dilation?

options.A: Mild scratchy throat sensation
options.B: Slight fatigue from the sedation
options.C: Temporary change in voice pitch
options.D: Fever and severe worsening pain

explanation: A little throat scratchiness is totally normal after having tools passed down. But fever and severe, getting-worse pain mean infection or a tear, which need immediate care.

question: What is the best diet to start a patient on right after they go home from an esophageal dilation?

options.A: Consume only dry cracker products for the first three days
options.B: Maintain strict total parenteral nutrition for one full week
options.C: Resume regular heavy solid meals immediately to test the stretch
options.D: Start with clear liquids and slowly advance to soft foods

explanation: The lining of the esophagus needs a little time to calm down. Starting with clear liquids gives it a break before slowly moving up to soft, easy-to-swallow foods.

question: What is the primary clinical indication for initiating nasogastric tube feeding?

options.A: Immediate decompression of the large colon
options.B: Inability to ingest adequate oral nutrients safely
options.C: A non-functioning gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Permanent total parenteral nutrition failure

explanation: Nasogastric tube feeding is utilized when the gut works fine, but the patient cannot safely swallow or eat enough food by mouth. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is a nasogastric tube contraindicated in a patient with severe mid-facial fractures?

options.A: Enteral feeds cannot pass through fractured nasal bones
options.B: Gastric acid production will instantly melt the plastic
options.C: The tube risks misplacement into the cranial vault
options.D: The fracture prevents proper stomach digestion

explanation: Severe trauma to the cribriform plate or mid-face creates a risk that a nasally inserted tube could enter the brain rather than the esophagus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: What should be assessed on the patient's nose prior to nasogastric tube insertion?

options.A: Presence of facial hair and sinus tenderness
options.B: Sense of smell and cranial nerve function
options.C: Patency and airflow of both nasal passages
options.D: Skin temperature and capillary refill time

explanation: Checking nostril patency ensures the clinician selects the clearer nasal passage for easier passage and less trauma. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: How does an alert patient actively assist during the insertion of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: By holding their breath for long intervals
options.B: By swallowing water or saliva as the tube advances
options.C: By guiding the tube down the throat with their fingers
options.D: By coughing continuously to open the airway

explanation: Swallowing closes the trachea and opens the esophagus, facilitating smooth passage of the tube into the stomach rather than the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: What anatomical landmarks are used to measure the correct insertion length of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Center of forehead to chin to umbilicus
options.B: Eyebrow to sternal notch to pubic bone
options.C: Lip to clavicle to lower rib cage
options.D: Nose to earlobe to xiphoid process

explanation: This traditional measurement estimates the distance from the entry point through the esophagus to the upper stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: A patient starts coughing violently, turns cyanotic, and gasps for air while a nurse is advancing a nasogastric tube. What is the immediate action?

options.A: Push the tube in faster to bypass the vocal cords
options.B: Ask the patient to speak louder to test airflow
options.C: Instill 30 milliliters of sterile water to check clearing
options.D: Withdraw the tube immediately and allow recovery

explanation: Coughing and cyanosis strongly indicate that the tube has entered the respiratory tract instead of the esophagus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is considered the definitive gold standard method for verifying nasogastric tube placement?

options.A: Auscultating air injected into the stomach
options.B: Observing the patient's respiratory rate
options.C: Obtaining an abdominal X-ray
options.D: Measuring the external length of the tubing

explanation: Radiographic imaging provides clear visual proof of where the tip of the feeding tube rests inside the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which pH range of fluid aspirated from a newly inserted tube provides strong evidence of gastric placement?
explanation: Gastric fluid is highly acidic due to hydrochloric acid, yielding a low pH reading typically between 1.0 and 4.0. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the recommended minimum elevation for the head of a patient's bed during nasogastric tube feeding?

options.A: 10 degrees
options.B: 30 to 45 degrees
options.C: Flat horizontal position
options.D: 60 to 75 degrees

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed utilizes gravity to reduce the risk of regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is regular water flushing performed through a nasogastric feeding tube?

options.A: To stimulate immediate bowel movements
options.B: To prevent tube clogging and maintain patency
options.C: To replace lost gastric hydrochloric acid
options.D: To cool down warm liquid formulas

explanation: Water flushes clear residual formula and medications from the inner lumen of the tube, preventing blockages. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which of the following is a common local mechanical complication of nasogastric tube use?

options.A: Enlargement of the thyroid gland
options.B: Spontaneous rupture of the esophagus
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste
options.D: Pressure necrosis of the nasal mucosa

explanation: Continuous pressure from the tube and securement tape against the naris can cause localized skin breakdown and tissue ischemia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of diarrhea in a patient receiving continuous enteral tube feedings?

options.A: Excessive daily water flushes
options.B: Elevating the head of the bed too high
options.C: Using a polyurethane tube instead of silicone
options.D: Rapid administration rate or high formula osmolarity

explanation: Hyperosmolar formulas or rapid delivery can overwhelm intestinal absorption capacity, leading to osmotic diarrhea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: What breathing instruction should be given to a patient just before removing a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Take a deep breath and hold it
options.B: Exhale completely and cough hard
options.C: Breathe rapidly through the mouth
options.D: Take short shallow breaths

explanation: Holding the breath closes the glottis, protecting the airway from accidental aspiration of any residual fluid as the tube comes out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why must the nurse inspect the tip of the nasogastric tube immediately after removal?

options.A: To calculate the total caloric intake delivered
options.B: To verify that the entire tube was removed intact
options.C: To measure the exact pH of the terminal end
options.D: To sterilize it for the next patient use

explanation: Inspecting the tip ensures no fragments broke off and were left behind in the esophagus or stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a urinary catheter?

options.A: To deliver fluids directly into the kidneys
options.B: To prevent the formation of kidney stones
options.C: To drain urine from the bladder
options.D: To measure the capacity of the ureters

explanation: A catheter is a flexible tube inserted through the urethra specifically to allow urine to drain out of the bladder when a patient cannot do so naturally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why do nurses try to avoid using a urinary catheter unless it's truly necessary?

options.A: It brings a high risk of introducing bacteria into the urinary tract
options.B: It is extremely painful for every patient who receives one
options.C: It requires surgical removal by a urologist
options.D: It permanently weakens the bladder muscles within hours

explanation: You got it! Because catheters bypass the body's natural defenses, they easily let germs in, making infections a big risk. That's why we only use them when we really have to.

question: Which body feature makes female patients more likely to get a catheter-related urinary tract infection?

options.A: A wider urethral opening
options.B: A larger bladder capacity than males
options.C: An absence of a muscular sphincter
options.D: A shorter urethra close to the anal opening

explanation: Spot on! The female urethra is quite short and sits very close to the anus, giving bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder.

question: How is putting a catheter into a male patient different from a female patient?

options.A: It lacks a sphincter muscle, making insertion completely effortless
options.B: It opens directly into the abdominal cavity
options.C: It is longer and has natural curves that require careful maneuvering
options.D: It is wider, requiring much larger catheter sizes

explanation: Exactly! The male urethra is longer and travels through the prostate, so you have to gently navigate a few natural bends during the procedure.

question: What keeps a Foley catheter securely in place inside the bladder?

options.A: A flexible wire attached to the belly wall
options.B: External adhesive tape on the thigh
options.C: Natural suction created by the drainage bag
options.D: A water-filled balloon at the tip

explanation: Correct! Once the catheter is inside the bladder, sterile water fills a tiny balloon at the end, acting like an anchor so it doesn't slip out.

question: When would you choose a simple straight catheter instead of a permanent Foley catheter?

options.A: When the patient is unconscious in the intensive care unit
options.B: When a patient needs periodic bladder emptying without a permanent bag
options.C: When the patient has a severe urethral blockage
options.D: When long-term continuous monitoring of hourly urine output is required

explanation: You nailed it! Straight catheters are popped in to drain the bladder and taken right back out, which lowers the risk of infection compared to leaving a tube in all day.

question: Which of these is a valid medical reason to put in an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: General urinary incontinence with no skin breakdown
options.B: To make things easier for nursing staff during busy night shifts
options.C: Accurate hourly urine output measurement in a critically ill patient
options.D: The patient prefers not to get up to use the toilet at night

explanation: Spot on! We only use indwelling catheters when there is a strong medical need, like closely tracking kidney function in very sick patients.

question: A patient with an enlarged prostate hasn't peed in eight hours and has severe lower belly pain. What should you do first?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink more water to flush the system
options.B: Administer a mild oral water pill (diuretic)
options.C: Prepare equipment for urinary catheterisation as ordered
options.D: Apply a warm compress to the lower back and wait two hours

explanation: Great thinking! When urine gets trapped because of an enlarged prostate, getting it out with a catheter right away relieves the painful pressure.

question: What common allergy must you always check for before using a standard urinary catheter?

options.A: Sulfonamides
options.B: Aspirin
options.C: Penicillin
options.D: Latex

explanation: You got it! Many standard catheters contain latex, which can cause severe allergic reactions. Always check your patient's history and grab a silicone one if they are allergic!

question: Why is it helpful to feel (palpate) the patient's lower belly before doing a catheterisation?

options.A: To stimulate the urethral sphincter to open
options.B: To check if the kidneys are infected
options.C: To measure the exact length of the urethra
options.D: To confirm the presence of a full, distended bladder

explanation: Spot on! Feeling the lower belly (suprapubic area) lets you check if urine is actually backed up and trapped in the bladder, confirming you really need to catheterize.

question: In what direction should you clean a female patient's perineal area before putting in a catheter?

options.A: From back to front
options.B: From side to side vigorously
options.C: From front to back
options.D: In a circular outward motion

explanation: Correct! Always wipe from front to back (toward the back passage) so you don't drag any germs from the anus toward the urethral opening.

question: In male patients, why must you push the catheter a bit further in even after urine first starts to flow?

options.A: To clear any leftover bacteria sitting in the outer urethra
options.B: To make the drainage bag fill up much faster
options.C: To stretch the urethral muscle and reduce future spasms
options.D: To ensure the retention balloon is completely inside the bladder before inflating it

explanation: Spot on! If you inflate the balloon while it's still stuck in the narrow urethra instead of the open bladder, it causes terrible pain and injury.

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed at all times?

options.A: Level with the patient's hips
options.B: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.C: Hanging from the top of the bed frame
options.D: Below the level of the bladder

explanation: You got it! Gravity is our friend here. Keeping the bag lower than the bladder keeps urine flowing smoothly downward and stops dirty urine from washing back up.

question: What is the main danger of disconnecting the catheter tubing from the drainage bag?

options.A: It breaks the closed system and lets bacteria enter
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions to the plastic
options.C: It causes immediate permanent damage to the urethral sphincter
options.D: It creates high pressure that bursts the balloon

explanation: Spot on! Keeping the drainage system sealed and closed is the single best way to protect your patient from getting a catheter-associated infection.

question: What should you check first if a patient with a catheter suddenly stops passing urine?

options.A: Pull the catheter out right away and put in a new one
options.B: Give a fast dose of an intravenous water pill
options.C: Check the tubing for kinks, twists, or someone lying on it
options.D: Call the doctor to report total kidney failure

explanation: Great nursing instinct! Most of the time, urine stops flowing simply because the tube is bent or pinched. Always check the lines first!

question: Which sign is a strong indicator of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.A: Cloudy and foul-smelling urine
options.B: Extreme dryness of the mouth
options.C: Bright red blood in the stool
options.D: Sudden swelling of the lower legs

explanation: You nailed it! When urine turns cloudy, smells bad, or the patient feels feverish and uncomfortable, it usually points to a brewing infection.

question: How do you deflate the retention balloon before taking out a Foley catheter?

options.A: Puncture the outer catheter wall with a large needle
options.B: Cut the balloon valve tubing with surgical scissors
options.C: Inject more water to pop the balloon safely inside the bladder
options.D: Attach a syringe to the inflation port and draw out all the water

explanation: Spot on! Hooking up a syringe and pulling out the exact amount of water that was put in ensures the balloon collapses completely before you slide the tube out.

question: What is an important task to carry out after a patient's urinary catheter is removed?

options.A: Keep the patient on strict bed rest for a full day
options.B: Monitor and measure the time and amount of their first pee
options.C: Give routine antibiotic pills to every patient
options.D: Restrict fluid intake for twelve hours to give the bladder a rest

explanation: You got it! Watching to see that they successfully pee within a reasonable time proves their bladder is waking up and working normally after catheter removal.

question: Why is there a small balloon near the tip of an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: To open up a blocked urethral passage
options.B: To measure the pressure inside the bladder
options.C: To hold the catheter securely inside the bladder
options.D: To prevent bacteria from traveling up the tube

explanation: Great job! Once water goes into that tiny balloon, it acts like an anchor so the tube stays safely put without slipping out.

question: When is using an indwelling catheter most necessary?

options.A: To treat a mild, uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection
options.B: For managing stress incontinence during daytime activities
options.C: As a convenient alternative for an elderly patient who dislikes walking
options.D: For accurate urine output monitoring in a critically ill patient

explanation: Spot on! Catheters carry infection risks, so we save them for serious needs like critical care, surgery, or major retention—not just for convenience.

question: About how long is the adult female urethra?

options.A: 12 centimeters
options.B: 4 centimeters
options.C: 20 centimeters
options.D: 30 centimeters

explanation: You've got this! The female urethra is quite short (about 4 cm), which makes catheterization quick, though it also means bacteria have a shorter trip to cause trouble.

question: Oops! During insertion, your catheter accidentally slips into the female vagina. What should you do next?

options.A: Wash the same catheter with antiseptic soap and try again
options.B: Leave it temporarily as a landmark and insert a new sterile catheter
options.C: Push it deeper into the vagina to find the correct opening
options.D: Remove it and immediately push that same tube into the urethral meatus

explanation: Smart nursing move! Leaving that stray tube in the vagina stops you from accidentally making the same mistake twice on your next try.

question: What does the French (Fr) scale tell you about a urinary catheter?

options.A: The outer diameter of the catheter tube
options.B: The maximum volume of the retention balloon
options.C: The total length of the drainage tubing
options.D: The rigidity of the catheter material

explanation: Think of the French size as the thickness of the tube. The bigger the number, the wider the catheter!

question: Why would a patient need a triple-lumen catheter for continuous bladder irrigation?

options.A: It increases the French size automatically during surgery
options.B: It provides separate channels for drainage, balloon inflation, and fluid instillation
options.C: It prevents the patient from accidentally pulling the tube out
options.D: It allows three nurses to flush the bladder simultaneously

explanation: Exactly! Three separate pathways mean fluid can flow in, urine can flow out, and the balloon stays inflated all at the same time.

question: Before opening a standard catheter kit, which major allergies must you always check for?

options.A: Penicillin and sulfa
options.B: Latex and iodine
options.C: Insulin and heparin
options.D: Paracetamol and aspirin

explanation: Always double-check! Standard kits usually contain latex tubing and iodine cleansers, so catching an allergy early saves your patient a lot of pain.

question: Why should you check for bladder fullness using a scanner or your hands before placing a catheter?

options.A: To numb the urethral canal before inserting the tube
options.B: To confirm there is an actual need to drain urine before invading sterile tissue
options.C: To measure the exact concentration of bacteria inside the bladder
options.D: To determine what size French catheter is required

explanation: Brilliant! Because catheters bring infection risks, we only want to insert one when we are certain the patient's bladder is actually holding urine.

question: When cleaning the female urethral area with antiseptic swabs, which direction should you wipe?

options.A: In a circular scrubbing motion
options.B: From side to side repeatedly
options.C: From back to front
options.D: From front to back

explanation: Always wipe from cleanest to dirtiest—front to back! This keeps nasty bacteria away from the urinary opening.

question: Your patient cries out in sharp pain as you inflate the catheter balloon. What is your very first move?

options.A: Stop inflation immediately and check if the catheter is still in the urethra
options.B: Push the catheter in harder to reach the proper depth
options.C: Inject the remaining water quickly to finish the procedure
options.D: Administer an oral painkiller and continue inflating

explanation: Stop right away! Pain during balloon inflation usually means the balloon is stuck inside the narrow urethra instead of resting safely in the bladder.

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed relative to the patient's bladder at all times?

options.A: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.B: Below the level of the bladder
options.C: Level with the mattress surface
options.D: Hanging from the top bed rail

explanation: Gravity is your friend here! Keeping the bag lower than the bladder stops urine from flowing backward and causing an infection.

question: Why is it important to tape or strap the catheter tubing to the patient's thigh?

options.A: It prevents pulling and friction injuries inside the fragile urethral canal
options.B: It eliminates the need for daily perineal hygiene care
options.C: It speeds up the rate of urine production from the kidneys
options.D: It prevents the drainage bag from filling up too quickly

explanation: Spot on! Securing the tube stops body movements from tugging on it, protecting delicate tissues from painful friction.

question: What is the single best way to prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?

options.A: Clamp the catheter for two hours every afternoon
options.B: Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer medically necessary
options.C: Apply antibiotic ointment around the meatus three times a day
options.D: Disconnect the drainage tubing every morning to flush it out

explanation: You've got it! The golden rule of preventing catheter infections is taking the tube out the moment it's no longer needed.

question: Why is breaking the seal of a closed urinary drainage system a bad idea?

options.A: It stops urine production in the kidneys
options.B: It causes the retention balloon to deflate spontaneously
options.C: It changes the French size of the catheter tubing
options.D: It allows bacteria to enter the system and travel directly into the bladder

explanation: Keep that system closed! Breaking the seal opens a wide-open highway for germs to march straight up into the bladder.

question: Your catheterized patient has had no urine output for two hours and feels lower belly discomfort. What do you check first?

options.A: Check the tubing for kinks, twists, or compression under the patient
options.B: Call the doctor to report acute kidney failure
options.C: Remove the catheter immediately and insert a new one
options.D: Inject sterile water into the balloon to secure it further

explanation: Always look for the simple fix first! A twisted or flattened tube is usually the culprit when urine suddenly stops flowing.

question: What does a nurse suspect when thick blood clots keep blocking a urinary catheter?

options.A: Complete failure of the patient's kidneys to filter blood
options.B: An allergic reaction to the latex material of the drainage bag
options.C: Internal obstruction of the lumen requiring patency check or irrigation
options.D: A normal healing process that requires no nursing intervention

explanation: Clots and debris can clog up the inside of the tube like a blocked drain, meaning you'll need to check if it's patent or flush it.

question: What crucial step must you never forget before pulling out an indwelling catheter?

options.A: Completely deflate the balloon by withdrawing all the sterile water with a syringe
options.B: Apply heat packs to the patient's lower abdomen
options.C: Clamp the catheter for 24 hours to exercise the bladder
options.D: Disconnect the drainage bag and flush the tube with antiseptic solution

explanation: Never skip this! Pulling out a catheter while the balloon is still full will cause severe, painful injury to the patient.

question: What is an important thing to monitor after you take out a patient's catheter?

options.A: Insert a new catheter immediately to prevent infection
options.B: Monitor and document the patient's first spontaneous urination within 6 to 8 hours
options.C: Ensure the patient drinks at least five liters of water in the first hour
options.D: Check the patient's blood pressure every fifteen minutes

explanation: You're doing great! Watching for that first pee lets you know the bladder is waking back up and helps catch any post-removal retention early.

question: Why do surgeons place a surgical drain inside a wound after an operation?

options.A: To keep the patient completely immobile during recovery
options.B: To prevent fluid and blood from collecting inside the wound
options.C: To deliver strong liquid antibiotics directly into tissues
options.D: To speed up the healing of skin stitches

explanation: You've got this! Drains are simply there to stop blood or serum from forming nasty pockets that could lead to an infection. Great clinical thinking!

question: What is the main goal of using a chest drain to remove air or fluid from the chest cavity?

options.A: It restores negative pressure to help the lung expand properly
options.B: It prevents the patient from coughing up mucus
options.C: It directly cleans the inner lining of the bronchial tubes
options.D: It stops the heart from beating too fast during stress

explanation: Spot on! When air or fluid gets trapped in the chest, it breaks the natural vacuum (negative pressure) and causes the lung to collapse. The chest drain fixes that vacuum.

question: Which of these is a classic example of an open drainage system?

options.A: Jackson-Pratt bulb
options.B: Hemovac evacuator
options.C: Penrose drain
options.D: Foley catheter bag

explanation: A Penrose drain is an open system that lets fluid drain straight onto dressings because it doesn't have a sealed container. Easy peasy!

question: Why do modern surgical wards prefer closed drainage systems over open ones?

options.A: They completely stop the patient from feeling any surgical pain
options.B: They significantly lower the risk of outside bacteria entering the body
options.C: They allow the surgical wound to heal without any dressings at all
options.D: They never require the nurse to empty or measure the collected fluid

explanation: Think of closed systems as sealed packages—because they are closed to the outside air, germs have a much harder time getting in to cause an infection.

question: What is the primary purpose of using a nasogastric (NG) tube for gastric decompression?

options.A: To remove fluid, gas, and contents from the stomach
options.B: To remove blood collections from inside the chest cavity
options.C: To supply oxygen into the upper airway passages
options.D: To drain excess urine directly from the bladder

explanation: Correct! 'Decompression' just means taking the pressure off. An NG tube sucks out built-up gas and fluid so the stomach can rest and the patient won't vomit.

question: What keeps a Foley urinary catheter securely in place inside the bladder?

options.A: Special surgical glue applied to the inner thigh skin
options.B: A tight plastic clamp attached around the external tubing
options.C: An inflated water balloon near the catheter tip
options.D: Natural suction created by the urine collection bag

explanation: Brilliant! Once the catheter is inside the bladder, we fill a tiny balloon with sterile water so it acts like an anchor and won't slip out.

question: A surgical drain was flowing nicely, but now it has suddenly stopped. What should you suspect first?

options.A: The body has miraculously stopped producing all normal inflammatory fluid
options.B: The collection container is now completely sterile and safe to remove
options.C: The surgical wound has finished healing completely on its own
options.D: The tube might be blocked or kinked inside or outside the patient

explanation: When output stops abruptly, don't assume a miracle healing! Always check the tubing first for a clot, mucus, or a pesky kink.

question: Which sign around a surgical drain insertion site tells you an infection might be starting?

options.A: Normal skin color with slight firmness around the tube
options.B: Clear pink fluid on a dry, intact outer gauze
options.C: Foul-smelling pus and surrounding skin redness
options.D: A small drop of dried blood near the stitches

explanation: Spot on! Redness, warmth, swelling, and foul-smelling pus are classic signs that bacteria are multiplying. Time to alert the team!

question: While helping a patient walk, you notice their urine bag is hanging higher than their bladder. Why is this a problem?

options.A: Urine can flow backward into the bladder and cause an infection
options.B: The urine output will instantly turn bright red with blood
options.C: The plastic collection tubing will melt from body heat
options.D: The catheter balloon will automatically pop from the extra pressure

explanation: Gravity works both ways! If the bag is higher than the bladder, contaminated urine can flow right back inside and give the patient a nasty urinary tract infection.

question: Why must a nurse use a separate measuring cylinder for each patient when emptying drainage bags?

options.A: To stop the plastic containers from wearing out too quickly
options.B: To prevent cross-contamination and spread of infections between patients
options.C: To make measuring the fluid much faster during busy shifts
options.D: To ensure the hospital records look neat and well-organized

explanation: Infection control 101! Using dedicated equipment for every patient keeps germs from hitching a ride across the ward.

question: What is your very first action if a surgical drain accidentally falls completely out of a patient's wound?

options.A: Try to gently push the same tube right back into the hole
options.B: Leave the open wound uncovered so fresh air can dry it out
options.C: Cover the open site with a sterile dressing and notify the doctor
options.D: Wash the fallen tube with soap and tape it back onto the skin

explanation: Never try to push a fallen drain back in—that introduces germs! Instead, cover the site with a sterile dressing right away and call the doctor.

question: When a drainage tube gets blocked, which of these actions is completely WRONG and dangerous?

options.A: Pushing a partially dislodged tube back into the body cavity
options.B: Checking the entire length of the tubing for accidental kinks
options.C: Inspecting the tube for visible blood clots or mucus plugs
options.D: Notifying the medical team if output remains absent

explanation: You got it! Pushing a slipped tube back inside drags surface bacteria straight into sterile tissues. Always check with your senior or doctor first.

question: Why is a patient told to take a deep breath and hold it while a chest or surgical drain is being removed?

options.A: It increases pressure and prevents air from entering the body cavity
options.B: It completely stops the patient from feeling any discomfort at all
options.C: It relaxes the abdominal muscles so the stitches fall apart
options.D: It forces the remaining fluid to rush out before the hole seals

explanation: Holding the breath creates a little bit of internal pressure, stopping air from being sucked into the empty tract as the tube comes out.

question: What should you do immediately after a drain is successfully pulled out from a surgical wound?

options.A: Ask the patient to stand up and walk around the room
options.B: Leave the small hole open to the air so it dries quickly
options.C: Wash the open tract thoroughly with harsh antiseptic soap
options.D: Apply a sterile, airtight dressing over the insertion site

explanation: Always seal the site immediately with an airtight sterile dressing to protect the healing tissue and stop any air leaks or bleeding.

question: What is the main reason we do a bladder irrigation?

options.A: To stimulate voluntary control of the urethral sphincter
options.B: To measure the exact total daily kidney function
options.C: To permanently cure chronic urinary tract infections
options.D: To wash away debris and keep the catheter open

explanation: You're doing great! Flushing out small clots and sediment keeps urine flowing smoothly so the tube doesn't get blocked.

question: Why do doctors often order bladder irrigation right after prostate surgery?

options.A: To stretch the bladder muscle back to its normal size
options.B: To prevent dangerous blood clots from blocking urine drainage
options.C: To deliver strong pain medication directly into the bloodstream
options.D: To check if the kidneys are producing enough red blood cells

explanation: Spot on! Surgery areas tend to bleed a bit, and a steady flush stops clots from choking off the catheter.

question: When would you expect to see bladder irrigation actually ordered for a patient?

options.A: Mild urinary incontinence in an elderly resident
options.B: A routine change of a long-term Foley catheter
options.C: Gross hematuria with active blood clot formation
options.D: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection symptoms

explanation: When heavy blood and clots start blocking the catheter, irrigation is the go-to fix to clear the tube and get things moving again.

question: When should you as a nurse hold off on bladder irrigation unless the doctor specifically says it's okay?

options.A: When there is suspected trauma to the urinary tract
options.B: When urine output drops slightly over a two-hour window
options.C: When cloudy urine appears in the clear drainage tubing
options.D: When the patient reports mild burning around the meatus

explanation: Safety first! If the urinary tract is injured, pushing fluid in can force bacteria and fluid straight out into the pelvic tissue through the tear.

question: Why do we prefer a closed bladder irrigation system over an open one?

options.A: It allows the nurse to bypass the need for a physician order
options.B: It lowers the risk of introducing bacteria into the bladder
options.C: It prevents the patient from feeling any bladder spasms at all
options.D: It requires much less total fluid volume over twenty-four hours

explanation: Keeping everything connected means fewer germs can slip inside, which helps your patient avoid a nasty UTI.

question: What is the giveaway feature of a closed continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) setup?

options.A: Frequent manual disconnection of the drainage bag
options.B: A triple-lumen catheter with a dedicated inflow port
options.C: A syringe used every hour to flush out old urine
options.D: An open container collecting fluid at the bedside

explanation: That third lumen is a lifesaver—it hooks right up to the irrigation bag so fluid flows non-stop without breaking the sterile seal.

question: What kind of fluid do we usually use to irrigate a bladder?

options.A: Hydrogen peroxide mix
options.B: Dextrose five percent
options.C: Sterile normal saline
options.D: Tap water from the sink

explanation: You've got this! Sterile normal saline is isotonic, meaning it's gentle on the bladder lining and won't cause weird fluid shifts.

question: What should you warn your patient about right before you start a bladder irrigation?

options.A: Immediate drowsiness and heavy sleepiness
options.B: A strong urge to urinate or mild cramping
options.C: Numbness spreading down both upper legs
options.D: A sharp burning sensation in the lower back

explanation: No need to alarm them—just let them know that filling the bladder naturally tricks the body into feeling like it really needs to pee!

question: If you're running a CBI and the drainage suddenly turns bright red with clots, what should you do with the drip rate?

options.A: Slow down the fluid flow to let the bladder rest
options.B: Stop the irrigation completely and clamp the catheter
options.C: Increase the drip rate until the output turns lighter
options.D: Disconnect the drainage bag to drain the clots faster

explanation: Speed things up! Running the fluid faster helps wash out the fresh blood and clots before they block the tube completely.

question: Your CBI patient has bright red drainage and is crying out with severe lower tummy cramps. What's the most likely issue?

options.A: Rapid healing of the surgical wound inside the bladder
options.B: A blocked catheter trapping fluid and blood clots
options.C: A normal reaction to room-temperature saline solution
options.D: An allergic reaction to the antiseptic skin wipes

explanation: Think of it like a clogged sink: fluid keeps pouring in, but nowhere to go. This stretches the bladder and causes painful cramps.

question: During an open irrigation, what must you do immediately after disconnecting the catheter and tubing?

options.A: Flush the drainage bag with hot tap water
options.B: Ask the patient to stand up and walk around
options.C: Clean the floor around the bed with bleach
options.D: Protect both exposed ends with sterile caps

explanation: Always keep it sterile! Covering those open tips stops stray germs from jumping onto the connectors and into your patient.

question: While trying to do a manual flush, you feel a lot of resistance on the syringe plunger. What is your next move?

options.A: Push harder on the plunger to force the clot out
options.B: Inject twice as much fluid to clear the blockage
options.C: Pull the catheter halfway out of the urethra
options.D: Stop pushing immediately and report the resistance

explanation: Never force it! Pushing against a blockage can tear the delicate bladder wall or urethra. Stop and let the doctor know.

question: How do you figure out the true urine output for a patient who has continuous bladder irrigation running?

options.A: Measure only the dark red blood collected in the bag
options.B: Divide the total output volume by the number of hours
options.C: Add the amount of irrigation fluid to the total output
options.D: Subtract total fluid infused from total drainage output

explanation: Simple math: take everything in the drainage bag and minus the irrigation fluid you pumped in. What's left is pure urine from the kidneys!

question: What big problem happens if irrigation fluid keeps flowing into the bladder but refuses to drain out?

options.A: Sudden and permanent kidney failure
options.B: Extreme drop in body temperature
options.C: Bladder over-distension and severe pain
options.D: Severe swelling of the lower feet

explanation: If fluid gets trapped, the bladder walls stretch way too much, leading to major pain and potential tissue damage.

question: What key piece of information do you absolutely need to chart after a bladder irrigation shift?

options.A: The patient's favorite television show
options.B: The exact brand name of the IV pole
options.C: The net fluid balance for the shift
options.D: The weather outside the hospital room

explanation: Tracking the net fluid balance helps you keep a close eye on your patient's kidney function and overall safety.

question: Why is it important to write down the exact color and look of the drainage?

options.A: It helps track whether bleeding is resolving or worsening
options.B: It determines the exact antibiotic needed for an infection
options.C: It proves to the insurance company that the nurse was busy
options.D: It shows how much water the patient drank by mouth

explanation: Seeing the color shift from dark red to a clear pink lets you know if the surgical site is finally calming down.

question: What is the primary purpose of assisted feeding in a hospital setting?

options.A: To completely replace intravenous fluid administration therapy
options.B: To accelerate the physical digestion of solid foods in the stomach
options.C: To maintain or improve nutritional status when patients cannot feed themselves
options.D: To eliminate the need for routine nursing nutritional documentation

explanation: Assisted feeding bridges the gap when a patient's physical or cognitive state prevents independent oral intake, ensuring basic nutritional requirements are met. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: A patient with which condition is most likely to require direct nursing assistance during meal times?

options.A: Acute right-sided hemiparesis following a cerebrovascular accident
options.B: Uncomplicated uncomplicated essential hypertension well controlled on medication
options.C: Mild generalized anxiety disorder without any physical limitations
options.D: Healed lower limb fracture requiring use of crutches for ambulation

explanation: Neurological deficits like stroke often cause muscle weakness, paralysis, or coordination issues that impair a patient's ability to safely handle eating utensils. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why should a nurse offer the bedpan or urinal before serving a meal?

options.A: Urine elimination directly stimulates the physiological release of insulin
options.B: Hospital regulations strictly mandate toileting schedules before breakfast
options.C: Elimination needs can deplete energy required for eating and disrupt appetite
options.D: Bedpans placed near food trays interfere with nursing documentation tasks

explanation: Addressing elimination needs beforehand prevents unnecessary physical exhaustion and maintains a clean, comfortable environment conducive to eating. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is an important environmental intervention prior to assisting a visually impaired patient with feeding?

options.A: Feeding the patient in absolute silence to prevent sensory overload
options.B: Removing their corrective eyeglasses permanently to avoid lens smudging
options.C: Dimming the room lights completely to maximize their remaining peripheral vision
options.D: Describing the location of food items using the face of a clock analogy

explanation: Descriptive communication helps visually impaired patients locate their food independently and maintains their dignity during meals. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the recommended bed elevation angle for a patient receiving assisted oral feeding?

options.A: Low semi-Fowler position at 15 to 30 degrees
options.B: High Fowler position between 60 and 90 degrees
options.C: Trendelenburg position with feet elevated
options.D: Flat supine position at 0 degrees

explanation: An upright position uses gravity to direct food down the esophagus and away from the trachea, significantly reducing aspiration risk. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: How long should a patient remain upright after completing an assisted meal?

options.A: At least 30 minutes
options.B: Until the next shift begins
options.C: Exactly 5 minutes
options.D: No time is required

explanation: Remaining upright for half an hour prevents regurgitation and subsequent pulmonary aspiration while initial digestion begins. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h3)

question: What action should a nurse perform immediately before feeding a patient from a dietary tray?

options.A: Verify the diet ticket against the patient identification band
options.B: Document the meal intake percentage in the nursing notes
options.C: Administer all scheduled daily oral medications simultaneously
options.D: Brush the patient's teeth with fluoride toothpaste

explanation: Verifying patient identity and diet orders prevents dangerous errors, such as feeding a diabetic patient a high-sugar meal. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is it important to alternate solid food bites with small sips of fluid during a meal?

options.A: It artificially inflates the recorded daily fluid intake measurements
options.B: It rapidly dilutes gastric acid to prevent post-meal indigestion and cramping
options.C: It accelerates the total eating time to reduce nursing workload constraints
options.D: It helps clear residual food particles from the oral cavity and moistens dry food

explanation: Alternating fluids and solids prevents food from sticking in the throat or mouth, reducing the risk of choking and pocketing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which dietary modification is frequently prescribed for patients experiencing severe dysphagia?

options.A: High-fiber raw vegetable platters
options.B: Pureed foods and thickened liquids
options.C: Dry crackers and carbonated sodas
options.D: Large chunks of fibrous meat

explanation: Thickened liquids and pureed textures move more slowly and are easier to control, preventing premature spill into the airway for swallowing-impaired patients. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the best approach when assisting a patient with moderate dementia who becomes easily distracted during meals?

options.A: Leave the meal tray on the bedside table and walk away until they finish
options.B: Minimize environmental distractions and use simple, gentle verbal cues
options.C: Scold the patient firmly whenever they stop chewing to maintain focus
options.D: Forcefeed the entire meal rapidly before their attention span lapses

explanation: Reducing noise and providing calm, direct guidance helps keep cognitively impaired patients focused on the task of eating. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h5)

question: What specific information must a nurse document immediately after an assisted meal is finished?

options.A: The patient's preferred television channel during feeding
options.B: The exact market cost of the hospital meal ingredients
options.C: The name of the relative who prepared the home food
options.D: The estimated percentage of food and fluid consumed

explanation: Accurate documentation of nutritional intake allows the healthcare team to monitor caloric consumption and evaluate nutritional risk. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which finding should be reported to the medical team immediately following an assisted meal?

options.A: A small crumb falling onto the patient's hospital gown napkin
options.B: The patient requesting a warm cup of tea after finishing lunch
options.C: The patient expressing mild preference for rice over yam
options.D: Repeated coughing and throat clearing while swallowing liquids

explanation: Coughing during or after swallowing is a primary indicator of aspiration, requiring prompt clinical evaluation and potential dietary revision. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T3#GNS212_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary anatomical destination for formulas delivered via a gastrostomy tube?

options.A: The duodenum
options.B: The jejunum
options.C: The stomach
options.D: The esophagus

explanation: A gastrostomy tube is surgically placed directly through the abdominal wall into the stomach chamber. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is enteral nutrition via gastrostomy generally preferred over parenteral nutrition when the digestive tract works?

options.A: It preserves gut mucosal integrity and barrier function
options.B: It digests foods much faster than normal chewing
options.C: It completely eliminates the risk of aspiration pneumonia
options.D: It requires sterile central venous line insertion daily

explanation: Using the natural digestive tract maintains mucosal immunity and prevents bacterial translocation from the gut. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which gastrostomy device lies flat against the abdominal wall and is often chosen for active patients?

options.A: Nasogastric weighted feeding tube
options.B: Standard PEG tube with rigid bolster
options.C: Surgically placed open rubber catheter
options.D: Low-profile button device

explanation: Low-profile button devices minimize snagging on clothing and offer increased mobility for active individuals. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h2)

question: What holds a standard percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube securely inside the gastric lumen?

options.A: Adhesive tape wrapped tightly on the abdomen
options.B: Sutures tied tightly around the outer skin
options.C: An internal retention bolster or balloon
options.D: Gravity pulling down against the stomach wall

explanation: An internal bumper or water-filled balloon prevents the tube from accidentally pulling out of the stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h2)

question: At what angle should the head of the bed be maintained during and after a gastrostomy feeding?

options.A: 90 degrees upright
options.B: 30 to 45 degrees
options.C: Flat on the mattress
options.D: 15 degrees Trendelenburg

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to prevent regurgitation and aspiration of stomach contents into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: A nurse auscultates the abdomen of a patient with a gastrostomy tube before feeding. What is the main purpose of this action?

options.A: To confirm the presence of bowel sounds and motility
options.B: To test for upper airway respiratory congestion
options.C: To measure the exact pH of the gastric contents
options.D: To check if the internal balloon is fully inflated

explanation: Bowel sounds indicate that the gastrointestinal tract is active and capable of processing the administered formula. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is a key characteristic of a bolus gastrostomy feeding method?

options.A: Administration limited strictly to sterile water flushes
options.B: Slow continuous infusion running over twenty-four hours
options.C: Large volumes delivered quickly over a short duration
options.D: Continuous automated delivery using an electronic pump

explanation: Bolus feeds mimic normal meals by giving larger amounts of formula over a brief period, usually 15 to 20 minutes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h4)

question: When is an electric infusion pump typically selected for delivering gastrostomy nutrition?

options.A: When the nurse needs to finish all medications in under two minutes
options.B: When bolus feedings are too cheap for the hospital pharmacy budget
options.C: When the patient requires slow, continuous delivery to improve tolerance
options.D: When the patient wants to ambulate freely without any equipment

explanation: Continuous pumps are used when patients struggle to tolerate rapid volume loads in their stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of flushing a gastrostomy tube with water after administering a feed?

options.A: To cool down warm formula before it enters the gastric lumen
options.B: To test if the internal retention balloon has ruptured
options.C: To rapidly rehydrate the patient through the stomach lining
options.D: To prevent formula buildup and subsequent tube clogging

explanation: Water flushes clear residual thick formula from the inner walls of the tube, keeping the lumen patent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which cleansing agent should nurses generally avoid when performing routine care on a healed gastrostomy stoma site?

options.A: Full-strength hydrogen peroxide
options.B: Warm tap water and mild soap
options.C: Clean soft washcloths and air drying
options.D: Normal saline solution wipes

explanation: Harsh chemicals like hydrogen peroxide can destroy healthy granulation tissue and impede the healing process. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why should sustained-release or enteric-coated tablets never be crushed for gastrostomy administration?

options.A: Altering their form destroys their specialized release mechanism
options.B: The nursing pharmacist charges extra fees for crushed pills
options.C: Crushed pills taste extremely bitter if they touch the tongue
options.D: They will instantly dissolve into clear liquid without water

explanation: Crushing enteric-coated or sustained-release drugs causes a dangerous rapid surge of medication absorption into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: A nurse prepares to give three different liquid medications through a gastrostomy tube. What is the correct technique?

options.A: Crush all three tablets together and stir them into cold fruit juice
options.B: Administer each medication separately with water flushes between them
options.C: Infuse all medications at once without any water flushes in between
options.D: Mix all three medications together into the hanging formula bag

explanation: Giving drugs separately and flushing between them prevents adverse drug-drug interactions and avoids tube clogs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h6)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if a patient develops coughing and shortness of breath during a gastrostomy feed?

options.A: Stop the feeding immediately
options.B: Inject 50 mL of air into the tube
options.C: Increase the pump rate to finish faster
options.D: Lower the head of the bed flat

explanation: Coughing and dyspnea suggest potential pulmonary aspiration, requiring immediate cessation of the feed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary cause of a clogged gastrostomy tube?

options.A: Using warm water instead of cold water for flushes
options.B: Rotating the external retention bolster every morning
options.C: Inadequate flushing or unapproved crushed medications
options.D: Leaving the head of the bed elevated at 45 degrees

explanation: Formula residue accumulation and poorly dissolved medications are the leading causes of mechanical tube occlusion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why is accidental dislodgement of a gastrostomy tube considered an urgent clinical situation for home caregivers?

options.A: The stoma tract can begin to close rapidly within hours
options.B: The patient will immediately starve to death in ten minutes
options.C: Formula will explode across the room from gastric pressure
options.D: Insurance companies will cancel coverage for a new tube

explanation: Gastrostomy tracts heal and contract quickly, making prompt replacement essential to keep the route open. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h8)

question: What method best ensures that a family caregiver has truly mastered gastrostomy tube care before discharge?

options.A: Handing them a pre-printed pamphlet on discharge day
options.B: Verbal confirmation that they watched an online video
options.C: Requiring a hands-on return-demonstration of the skills
options.D: Asking the caregiver to read a twenty-page textbook chapter

explanation: Return-demonstration allows the nurse to directly observe technique and correct any errors before home management begins. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T4#GNS212_U1_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary function of the large intestine in bowel elimination?

options.A: Absorption of water and electrolytes
options.B: Secretion of digestive enzymes
options.C: Production of intrinsic factor
options.D: Initial breakdown of dietary proteins

explanation: The colon primarily extracts water and mineral electrolytes from remaining semi-solid chyme before excretion. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary physiological consequence of impaired mass peristalsis in the colon?

options.A: Inability to absorb dietary fats
options.B: Rapid transit causing watery diarrhea
options.C: Excessive water absorption leading to hard stool
options.D: Complete failure of protein digestion

explanation: When colonic transit slows down, more water is extracted from the stool, resulting in constipation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the term for a severe accumulation of hardened stool wedged in the rectum?

options.A: Paralytic ileus
options.B: Steatorrhea
options.C: Fecal impaction
options.D: Bowel obstruction

explanation: Fecal impaction occurs when unrelieved constipation allows dry, hard stool to accumulate and block the rectal vault. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h2)

question: A patient taking strong opioid pain medications is at high risk for developing which bowel complication?

options.A: Steatorrhea
options.B: Constipation
options.C: Malabsorption
options.D: Incontinence

explanation: Opioids significantly slow down gastrointestinal motility by binding to receptors in the enteric nervous system, causing severe constipation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which physical assessment technique should be performed immediately after inspecting the abdomen?

options.A: Deep palpation
options.B: Auscultation
options.C: Light palpation
options.D: Percussion

explanation: Auscultation must precede palpation and percussion because pressing on the abdomen can alter bowel motility and falsely change bowel sound frequencies. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h3)

question: What finding during abdominal auscultation is characteristic of a paralytic ileus?

options.A: High-pitched rushing tinkling sounds
options.B: Absent or very hypoactive bowel sounds
options.C: Bruits over the renal arteries
options.D: Hyperactive gurgling sounds in all quadrants

explanation: A paralytic ileus involves a temporary cessation of peristalsis, resulting in silent or markedly diminished bowel sounds. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is a critical physiological risk associated with performing digital removal of a fecal impaction?

options.A: Vagal nerve stimulation leading to bradycardia
options.B: Acute onset of paralytic ileus
options.C: Immediate rupture of the descending colon
options.D: Sudden spikes in systemic blood pressure

explanation: Irritation of the rectal wall during manual disimpaction can stimulate the vagus nerve, potentially causing a dangerous drop in heart rate. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h4)

question: A bedridden elderly patient with chronic constipation refuses high-fiber foods. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Prepare the patient for an emergency colonoscopy
options.B: Administer a strong stimulant suppository immediately
options.C: Insert a rectal tube to decompress the lower bowel
options.D: Encourage small, frequent sips of water throughout the day

explanation: Fluid intake is a safe, foundational intervention to soften stool when dietary fiber is difficult to increase immediately. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the expected normal color of a healthy intestinal stoma?

options.A: Yellowish green
options.B: Dark purple
options.C: Pale white
options.D: Pink to red

explanation: A healthy stoma is rich in blood vessels and should appear pink or red, similar to the mucosal lining of the inner cheek. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which assessment finding in a newly created colostomy requires immediate notification of the surgical team?

options.A: Mild edema during the first postoperative day
options.B: Stoma protruding slightly above the skin
options.C: A dusky or black stoma color
options.D: Small amount of serosanguineous drainage

explanation: A dark or blackened stoma indicates compromised blood supply and impending tissue necrosis, which is a surgical emergency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T5#GNS212_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary function of the proximal colon during digestion?

options.A: Absorption of water and electrolytes
options.B: Initial breakdown of complex proteins
options.C: Production of intrinsic factor
options.D: Secretion of digestive enzymes

explanation: The proximal colon extracts water and mineral electrolytes from the liquid chyme, converting it into solid or semisolid fecal matter as it moves distally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h1)

question: What physiological event immediately triggers the conscious urge to defecate?

options.A: Acidification of the sigmoid colon
options.B: Rectal distension by fecal mass
options.C: Release of gastrin in the stomach
options.D: Contraction of the internal anal sphincter

explanation: When stool enters the rectum, the walls stretch, which stimulates sensory nerve endings and triggers the neural reflex creating the urge to evacuate. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which medication class is well-known for directly slowing colonic motility through enteric receptor binding?

options.A: Opioids
options.B: Diuretics
options.C: Antibiotics
options.D: Beta-blockers

explanation: Opioid analgesics bind to mu-opioid receptors in the gastrointestinal tract, inhibiting peristalsis and significantly increasing fluid absorption from stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: What characterizes pelvic floor dyssynergia as a cause of constipation?

options.A: Complete absence of colonic peristaltic waves
options.B: Paradoxical contraction of pelvic floor muscles during evacuation
options.C: Excessive secretion of mucus by the rectal mucosa
options.D: Rapid transit of stool through the transverse colon

explanation: In defecatory disorders, the muscles that should relax to allow passage instead tighten inappropriately, blocking the exit pathway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which symptom is considered a red flag requiring urgent investigation in a patient with new-onset constipation?

options.A: Mild lower abdominal bloating
options.B: Unexplained weight loss
options.C: Intermittent passage of gas
options.D: Occasional mild cramping

explanation: Unexplained weight loss, alongside rectal bleeding or anemia, strongly suggests an organic pathology like a malignancy rather than simple functional constipation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h3)

question: A digital rectal examination is performed on a patient complaining of severe constipation. What is a primary clinical purpose of this assessment?

options.A: To stimulate immediate high-amplitude peristaltic contractions
options.B: To collect a baseline sample for routine urinalysis
options.C: To evaluate sphincter tone and check for fecal impaction
options.D: To measure exact colonic transit time directly

explanation: Digital examination allows the clinician to feel the consistency of stool in the vault, check for masses, and assess resting and squeeze anal tone. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h3)

question: How do osmotic laxatives primarily relieve constipation?

options.A: By absorbing excess gas and softening the outer fecal coating
options.B: By directly irritating the colonic mucosa to speed up peristalsis
