options.C: By paralyzing the internal anal sphincter for easier passage
options.D: By drawing water into the intestinal lumen through osmotic pressure

explanation: Osmotic agents are poorly absorbed substances that retain fluid within the bowel lumen, keeping stools soft and bulky. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which classification of laxatives works best by directly stimulating myenteric nerve endings in the colon?

options.A: Saline enemas
options.B: Stimulant laxatives
options.C: Emollient softeners
options.D: Bulk-forming agents

explanation: Stimulants like senna increase intestinal motility by acting directly on the mucosal nerve plexuses of the large intestine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is it important to increase fluid intake when recommending a high-fiber diet to a patient?

options.A: To prevent the rapid breakdown of fiber into simple sugars
options.B: To activate the kidneys to produce hormones that stimulate peristalsis
options.C: To dilute digestive enzymes so they do not irritate the stomach lining
options.D: To prevent the fiber from forming a dense, obstructing mass in the bowel

explanation: Bulk-forming fiber requires sufficient water to swell properly; without adequate fluids, dry fiber can worsen constipation or cause impaction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient asks when is the best time to attempt having a bowel movement to take advantage of natural body rhythms. What is the best response?

options.A: Twenty to thirty minutes after finishing a meal
options.B: Right before going to bed at night
options.C: In the middle of the afternoon during peak activity
options.D: Immediately upon waking up before drinking anything

explanation: Eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which naturally increases colonic motility and creates an optimal window for successful evacuation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is a primary clinical consequence of a severe, prolonged fecal impaction?

options.A: Spontaneous healing of chronic anal fissures
options.B: Paradoxical overflow diarrhea around the mass
options.C: Rapid acceleration of upper gastrointestinal transit
options.D: Excessive production of pancreatic digestive enzymes

explanation: When hard stool blocks the rectum, liquid stool from higher up can slip around the impaction, presenting as sudden fecal incontinence or diarrhea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which preventive nursing action is most effective for a bedridden patient newly started on strong opioid therapy?

options.A: Initiating a prophylactic bowel regimen with stool softeners and stimulants
options.B: Encouraging heavy weightlifting exercises in bed
options.C: Waiting until the patient complains of pain before intervening
options.D: Restricting daily oral fluid intake to prevent bladder distension

explanation: Because opioids consistently slow bowel transit, proactive laxative therapy prevents constipation before it develops into impaction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h6)

question: What stool frequency defines diarrhoea clinically?

options.A: One hard, dry stool every two days
options.B: Three or more loose or liquid stools per day
options.C: Two formed stools daily with mucus
options.D: Passage of bloody stool once a week

explanation: The clinical definition relies on a frequency of three or more loose or liquid bowel movements within a twenty-four-hour period. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h1)

question: What distinguishes acute diarrhoea from chronic diarrhoea?

options.A: Presence or absence of fever
options.B: Duration of symptoms over time
options.C: Response to oral rehydration salt
options.D: Amount of blood in the stool

explanation: Acute diarrhoea resolves within two weeks, whereas chronic diarrhoea lasts for four weeks or longer, pointing to different underlying etiologies. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which mechanism of diarrhoea stops completely when the patient fasts or stops consuming the offending substance?

options.A: Osmotic diarrhoea
options.B: Inflammatory diarrhoea
options.C: Secretory diarrhoea
options.D: Exudative diarrhoea

explanation: Because osmotic diarrhoea is caused by unabsorbed solutes drawing water into the lumen, fasting removes the solute load and stops the fluid shift. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h2)

question: What causes secretory diarrhoea to persist even when a patient takes nothing by mouth?

options.A: Active ion secretion driven by toxins
options.B: Destruction of the anal sphincter
options.C: Mechanical obstruction of the colon
options.D: Rapid transit of undigested fats

explanation: Bacterial enterotoxins stimulate continuous ion and fluid secretion from the crypt cells into the gut lumen, independent of food intake. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a skin pinch test in a child with diarrhoea?

options.A: To assess the degree of dehydration
options.B: To determine the presence of intestinal parasites
options.C: To check for abdominal organomegaly
options.D: To measure baseline core body temperature

explanation: Skin turgor assessed via a pinch test evaluates fluid loss and helps grade the severity of dehydration in vulnerable patients. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h3)

question: What do visible blood and mucus in a diarrhoeal stool typically indicate?

options.A: Invasive mucosal inflammation
options.B: Simple viral gastroenteritis
options.C: Purely osmotic fluid shifts
options.D: Rapid bowel transit time

explanation: The presence of blood and mucus signifies damage to the intestinal mucosa caused by invasive bacterial or parasitic pathogens. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h3)

question: Which diagnostic test is most appropriate for identifying specific bacterial pathogens in a persistent case of diarrhoea?

options.A: Plain abdominal radiograph
options.B: Stool culture and sensitivity
options.C: Urinalysis and microscopy
options.D: Full blood count analysis

explanation: Stool cultures grow and isolate specific bacteria, allowing laboratories to test which antimicrobial agents will effectively treat the infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h4)

question: A patient with severe watery diarrhoea develops lethargy and muscle cramps. Which blood test is most crucial to run immediately?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: Fast blood glucose test
options.C: Liver enzyme panel
options.D: Serum electrolytes and renal function

explanation: Massive fluid loss leads to electrolyte depletion and acute kidney injury, making immediate electrolyte and creatinine checks vital. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why are antimotility drugs avoided in patients with invasive bacterial diarrhoea?

options.A: They trap toxins and worsen mucosal invasion
options.B: They increase the absorption of oral fluids
options.C: They immediately cause severe renal failure
options.D: They neutralize stomach acid production

explanation: Slowing bowel motility prevents the body from expelling harmful pathogens and toxins, prolonging the infection and increasing systemic complications. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which micronutrient supplement is recommended by health authorities to reduce the duration and severity of acute diarrhoea in young children?

options.A: Zinc
options.B: Iron
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Zinc supplementation restores intestinal absorptive function, boosts local immune responses, and shortens the clinical course of diarrhoeal illness in children. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h5)

question: What physiological mechanism makes Oral Rehydration Salts so effective for treating dehydration?

options.A: Inhibition of intestinal peristaltic waves
options.B: Direct absorption through the gastric lining
options.C: Stimulation of active bicarbonate secretion
options.D: Coupled sodium-glucose transport in the gut

explanation: Glucose molecules pull sodium ions across the intestinal brush border via co-transporters, which in turn drags water passively into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for applying barrier creams during nursing care for a patient with severe diarrhoea?

options.A: To reduce the frequency of bowel movements
options.B: To measure the exact volume of fecal output
options.C: To block the transcutaneous absorption of bacterial toxins
options.D: To prevent painful skin excoriation from acidic stools

explanation: Frequent watery stools irritate the perianal skin, making protective barrier ointments essential for maintaining skin integrity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct complication of severe, untreated acute diarrhoea?

options.A: Severe hypokalemia
options.B: Primary pulmonary hypertension
options.C: Acute kidney injury
options.D: Hypovolemic shock

explanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a cardiopulmonary disorder unrelated to the fluid and electrolyte depletion caused by acute diarrhoea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the most effective community-level preventative measure nurses should emphasize during health education talks on diarrhoeal diseases?

options.A: Strict long-term fasting during the rainy season
options.B: Proper handwashing with soap and clean water
options.C: Routine administration of prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Universal screening of stool for parasites

explanation: Hand hygiene interrupts the fecal-oral transmission route, which is the primary mode of spreading most enteric pathogens responsible for diarrhoea. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary clinical definition of faecal incontinence?

options.A: The inability to produce bowel movements for over a week
options.B: The recurrent involuntary passage of faecal material
options.C: The excessive production of intestinal gas causing abdominal distension
options.D: Painful defecation accompanied by bright red rectal bleeding

explanation: Faecal incontinence specifically refers to the loss of voluntary control over the evacuation of bowel contents. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is faecal incontinence often underreported by patients presenting to healthcare facilities?

options.A: Rapid resolution of symptoms without medical intervention
options.B: Deep-seated cultural stigma and embarrassment
options.C: Lack of available diagnostic tools in local clinics
options.D: Strict hospital policies limiting symptom discussion

explanation: Patients frequently hide bowel control issues due to the sensitive nature of the topic and fear of social ostracization. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which muscle forms a sling around the anorectal junction to maintain the acute anococcygeal angle?

options.A: Levator ani major muscle
options.B: Internal obturator muscle
options.C: Puborectalis muscle
options.D: Gluteus maximus muscle

explanation: The puborectalis muscle acts as a mechanical sling, pulling the rectum forward to maintain continence at rest. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the internal anal sphincter?

options.A: Secreting mucus to lubricate the lower anal canal
options.B: Providing voluntary squeezing during emergency defection
options.C: Detecting the chemical composition of passing gas
options.D: Maintaining resting anal tone through involuntary control

explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a smooth muscle that stays contracted continuously to prevent leakage when resting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is a leading cause of faecal incontinence among women in many Nigerian clinical settings?

options.A: Idiopathic degeneration of the descending colon
options.B: Congenital megacolon diagnosed in adulthood
options.C: Obstetric trauma from prolonged obstructed labor
options.D: Chronic use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

explanation: Difficult childbirths with perineal trauma or delayed medical interventions frequently damage the anal sphincter complex. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h3)

question: How do neurological conditions such as stroke contribute to the development of faecal incontinence?

options.A: By directly destroying the smooth muscle fibers of the rectal wall
options.B: By disrupting central nervous system control over bowel evacuation reflexes
options.C: By halting all mucus production within the large intestine
options.D: By causing permanent hyper-contraction of the internal anal sphincter

explanation: Stroke and spinal injuries impair the neural pathways required for conscious awareness and voluntary control of defecation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h3)

question: What characterizes passive faecal incontinence compared to urge incontinence?

options.A: Leakage occurs without the patient's conscious awareness
options.B: The patient experiences an intense, sudden urge to defecate
options.C: It is exclusively caused by acute bacterial infections
options.D: Symptoms only appear during strenuous physical exercise

explanation: Passive incontinence happens when sensory nerves fail to signal rectal filling or sphincters fail silently due to severe weakness. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h4)

question: A patient feels a sudden, urgent need to defecate but leaks stool before reaching the toilet. What type of incontinence is this?

options.A: Passive incontinence
options.B: Urge incontinence
options.C: Overflow incontinence
options.D: Neurogenic incontinence

explanation: This scenario describes urge incontinence, where the warning is felt, but the sphincter mechanism is too weak to hold back stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the clinical purpose of assessing the anal wink reflex during a physical examination?

options.A: To determine the moisture level of the perineal skin
options.B: To detect the presence of internal hemorrhoids
options.C: To evaluate the integrity of the S2-S4 sacral reflex arc
options.D: To measure the exact resting pressure of the internal sphincter

explanation: Stroking the perianal skin normally causes a reflex contraction of the external sphincter, proving intact sacral innervation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which tool is most appropriate for a nurse to use when assessing and recording a patient's stool consistency?

options.A: Braden Skin Scale
options.B: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.C: Apgar Scoring System
options.D: Bristol Stool Chart

explanation: The Bristol Stool Chart classifies human stool forms into seven distinct categories, aiding clinical communication regarding consistency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h5)

question: What physiological mechanism is utilized when scheduling bowel training after meals?

options.A: Enterogastric reflex
options.B: Cephalic phase response
options.C: Gastrocolic reflex
options.D: Peristaltic reversal

explanation: Eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which naturally increases colon motility and facilitates scheduled bowel evacuation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h6)

question: A patient undergoing pelvic floor muscle training for faecal incontinence keeps squeezing their buttocks and holding their breath. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Advise the patient to increase the weight resistance during the contraction phase
options.B: Switch the treatment plan immediately to commercial bulk-forming laxatives
options.C: Document that the patient has completed the pelvic floor exercise routine successfully
options.D: Correct the technique by instructing the patient to isolate the anal and perineal muscles

explanation: Effective pelvic floor training requires isolating the sphincter and puborectalis muscles rather than recruiting gluteal or abdominal muscles. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of perineal dermatitis in patients with faecal incontinence?

options.A: Irritation from fecal enzymes and prolonged moisture exposure
options.B: Fungal overgrowth caused by systemic antibiotic therapy
options.C: Mechanical friction from frequent ambulatory exercise
options.D: Allergic reactions to standard hospital-issued cotton linen

explanation: Enzymes present in stool combined with constant moisture breakdown the skin barrier, leading to painful inflammation and breakdown. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is it clinically recommended to pat dry rather than rub the perianal skin after cleansing?

options.A: To prevent the barrier ointment from sliding off the area
options.B: To ensure the skin absorbs residual moisture more rapidly
options.C: To avoid causing mechanical friction and further skin breakdown
options.D: To stimulate local blood circulation in the subcutaneous tissue

explanation: Fragile, macerated skin is highly susceptible to frictional damage, making gentle patting essential during hygiene care. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h7)

question: Which psychosocial challenge is most commonly reported by individuals living with chronic faecal incontinence?

options.A: Hyperactive mental alertness and mania
options.B: Pathological denial of physical symptoms
options.C: Social isolation and depression
options.D: Obsessive cleaning of public facilities

explanation: Fear of accidental soilage and embarrassment often drives patients to withdraw socially, leading to profound emotional distress. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is an effective nursing intervention to help manage the emotional impact of faecal incontinence?

options.A: Encouraging the patient to avoid all public outings indefinitely
options.B: Insisting that family members take over all personal hygiene tasks
options.C: Minimizing discussion of the topic to prevent further embarrassment
options.D: Creating a safe, non-judgmental space for open communication

explanation: Validating the patient's feelings and offering a compassionate environment helps reduce stigma and encourages adherence to care plans. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T8#GNS212_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of introducing barium sulfate into the large intestine during a barium enema?

options.A: To dissolve impacted fecal masses through enzymatic chemical action
options.B: To sterilize the colonic lumen prior to emergency surgical resection
options.C: To deliver therapeutic anti-inflammatory medication directly to ulcers
options.D: To provide a radiopaque coating that outlines the mucosal lining on X-rays

explanation: Barium sulfate is a dense contrast agent that blocks X-rays, allowing clear visualization of the internal contours of the colon. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h1)

question: When is a barium enema typically chosen over a standard colonoscopy in clinical practice?

options.A: When the patient cannot tolerate any form of liquid bowel preparation
options.B: When active lower gastrointestinal bleeding must be cauterized instantly
options.C: When a severe colonic stricture prevents the passage of an endoscope
options.D: When the patient requires immediate tissue biopsy of a mucosal lesion

explanation: Radiographic contrast can bypass narrow strictures that physically block the physical insertion of a flexible colonoscope. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which congenital condition in pediatric patients is frequently evaluated using a barium enema to reveal a narrow distal segment and a dilated proximal colon?

options.A: Hirschsprung's disease
options.B: Esophageal atresia
options.C: Pyloric stenosis
options.D: Necrotizing enterocolitis

explanation: Hirschsprung's disease involves the absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon, creating a characteristic transition zone visible on contrast studies. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h2)

question: What characteristic feature of ulcerative colitis is a barium enema particularly effective at revealing?

options.A: Loss of normal haustral markings and mucosal ulceration
options.B: Complete absence of the descending colon and rectum
options.C: Dilation of the superior mesenteric artery branches
options.D: Hypertrophy of the internal anal sphincter muscle

explanation: Chronic inflammation in ulcerative colitis alters the mucosal architecture, smoothing out haustral folds and showing ragged ulcer borders on contrast radiographs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary danger of introducing barium sulfate into the peritoneal cavity due to a bowel perforation?

options.A: Immediate systemic anaphylactic shock and airway closure
options.B: Permanent paralysis of the lower extremities from nerve toxicity
options.C: Rapid onset of iron-deficiency anemia and internal hemorrhage
options.D: Severe chemical peritonitis and granuloma formation

explanation: Extravasated barium acts as a severe chemical irritant in the peritoneal cavity, inciting intense inflammation and fibrous tissue reactions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which clinical scenario represents an absolute contraindication for a standard barium enema procedure?

options.A: Suspected acute colonic perforation
options.B: Mild, stable iron-deficiency anemia
options.C: Chronic intermittent lower abdominal cramping
options.D: History of uncomplicated internal hemorrhoids

explanation: Introducing contrast media into a perforated viscus allows barium to escape into the peritoneal cavity, triggering catastrophic peritonitis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h3)

question: Before scheduling a barium enema for a female patient of childbearing age, what critical assessment must the nurse perform?

options.A: Verify the patient's current pregnancy status
options.B: Assess the patient's ability to swallow large pills
options.C: Measure baseline fasting blood glucose levels
options.D: Check for a history of seasonal allergic rhinitis

explanation: Ionizing radiation and pelvic manipulation during fluoroscopy present significant risks to a developing fetus, making pregnancy verification mandatory. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is an important emotional and physical preparation detail the nurse should share with the patient?

options.A: The patient will feel strong cramping and an intense urge to expel the contrast
options.B: General anesthesia will be administered to keep the patient completely asleep
options.C: The procedure is entirely painless and requires no special breathing techniques
options.D: The patient must retain the barium inside their body for at least twenty-four hours

explanation: Warning patients about expected abdominal fullness, cramping, and defecation urges prevents panic during the fluoroscopic filling phase. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why is a strict clear liquid diet mandated the day before a barium enema?

options.A: To keep the stomach lining completely acidic for optimal contrast absorption
options.B: To prevent the patient from experiencing nausea during the driving trip
options.C: To minimize solid fecal residue that can mimic or obscure lesions on X-rays
options.D: To eliminate all gas pockets within the small intestine and stomach

explanation: Unremoved stool inside the colon creates filling defects on radiographs that can be easily mistaken for polyps or tumors. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h5)

question: A patient asks why colored gelatin or red fruit juices are prohibited during the clear liquid preparation phase. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Pigments can leave residues or mimic bleeding inside the mucosal lining
options.B: Dark colors block the X-ray beam just like dense metallic contrast agents
options.C: Artificial dyes bind permanently to barium and solidify the mixture
options.D: Sugar content in colored liquids causes severe immediate hyperglycemia

explanation: Artificial colorings and certain food pigments can be confused with pathological conditions or stain the bowel mucosa during preparation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h5)

question: In which position should the nurse place the patient initially for the safe insertion of the rectal tube during a barium enema?

options.A: Lithotomy position
options.B: Trendelenburg position
options.C: Sims' position
options.D: Supine flat position

explanation: The left lateral Sims' position allows natural relaxation of the anal sphincter and aligns with the anatomical curve of the rectosigmoid junction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h6)

question: What physiological complication must the nurse monitor for closely during the rapid filling of the colon with barium?

options.A: Acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilating in the dark room
options.B: Vasovagal response caused by bowel distension and cramping
options.C: Rapid onset of peripheral edema from fluid volume overload
options.D: Sudden malignant hypertension from increased intra-abdominal pressure

explanation: Rapid stretching of the bowel wall can stimulate the vagus nerve, causing sudden hypotension, dizziness, sweating, and bradycardia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h6)

question: What characteristic color change should the nurse inform the patient to expect in their stool following a barium enema?

options.A: Deep red with visible clots
options.B: Bright neon green or yellow
options.C: Chalky white or light gray
options.D: Jet black and tarry consistency

explanation: The elimination of residual barium sulfate pigment turns the stool a distinctive pale, chalky color for a couple of days after the test. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h7)

question: Why is increasing oral fluid intake a crucial post-procedure intervention after a barium enema?

options.A: To dissolve the remaining barium chemically inside the stomach
options.B: To stimulate the kidneys to filter out absorbed heavy metal toxins
options.C: To prevent the barium from solidifying and causing a severe fecal impaction
options.D: To replenish electrolytes lost during the intake of the contrast dye

explanation: Barium sulfate dries and hardens as water is absorbed by the colon; high fluid intake keeps the mixture soft and easily passable. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T9#GNS212_U1_T9_h7)

question: What is the main goal of performing CPR on a patient in cardiac arrest?

options.A: To cool down the body and protect the brain
options.B: To clear thick mucus from blocked airways
options.C: To restore normal heart rhythm immediately
options.D: To keep oxygenated blood flowing to vital organs

explanation: CPR acts as an artificial pump to circulate remaining oxygen in the blood to the brain and heart until advanced help arrives. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why is early initiation of CPR critical during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: It prevents permanent brain damage by maintaining minimal perfusion
options.B: It eliminates the need for any medications or defibrillation later
options.C: It completely cures the underlying heart disease causing the arrest
options.D: It guarantees the immediate return of spontaneous heartbeat

explanation: Brain cells begin to die within minutes without oxygen, so starting compressions quickly buys vital time. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h1)

question: What is the very first link in the adult chain of survival?

options.A: Early recognition and call for help
options.B: Immediate high-quality chest compressions
options.C: Rapid use of an automated external defibrillator
options.D: Advanced life support by paramedics

explanation: Recognizing an emergency and activating the emergency response system quickly starts the entire rescue process. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which link in the chain of survival specifically addresses restoring a shockable heart rhythm?

options.A: Post-cardiac arrest care
options.B: Rapid defibrillation
options.C: Early recognition and prevention
options.D: Advanced life support medication

explanation: Defibrillation delivers an electric shock to treat life-threatening rhythms like ventricular fibrillation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the very first step a nurse must take before starting CPR on a fallen person?

options.A: Attach the automated external defibrillator
options.B: Ensure the surrounding scene is safe
options.C: Open the airway with a head-tilt maneuver
options.D: Check the patient for a pulse

explanation: Rescuers must check for hazards like fire, live wires, or traffic so they do not become victims themselves. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient collapses in the hospital ward. What should the nurse do right after confirming the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally?

options.A: Leave the patient to find a doctor
options.B: Call for help and activate the emergency response
options.C: Administer rescue breaths through a mask
options.D: Start chest compressions immediately

explanation: Activating the emergency team immediately ensures that extra hands and equipment like an AED are on the way. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which maneuver is standardly used to open the airway of an unresponsive patient without a neck injury?

options.A: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
options.B: Jaw-thrust maneuver
options.C: Chest compression sweep
options.D: Recovery position roll

explanation: The head-tilt, chin-lift lifts the tongue away from the back of the throat to clear the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why should a nurse avoid pressing heavily on the soft tissue under the chin during the chin-lift maneuver?

options.A: it triggers an automatic reflex to vomit
options.B: It can push the tongue backward and block the airway
options.C: It forces stomach contents up into the mouth
options.D: It can cause permanent damage to the patient's jawbone

explanation: Pressing on the soft neck tissue collapses the airway instead of opening it, preventing proper breathing assessment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is the recommended compression rate per minute for performing adult CPR?

options.A: 80 to 100 compressions
options.B: 140 to 160 compressions
options.C: 60 to 80 compressions
options.D: 100 to 120 compressions

explanation: A rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute mimics an effective heart rate and maximizes blood flow. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why is complete chest recoil important between individual chest compressions?

options.A: It keeps the patient's lungs inflated with fresh air
options.B: It gives the rescuer's tired arm muscles a chance to rest
options.C: It prevents the ribs from fracturing during compressions
options.D: It lets the heart chambers fill back up with blood

explanation: If the chest does not recoil fully, the heart cannot refill properly, making the next compression useless. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h5)

question: What must all rescuers do immediately before an AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Clear the patient and ensure nobody is touching them
options.B: Check the patient's carotid pulse
options.C: Perform two quick rescue breaths
options.D: Turn the device power switch off

explanation: Rescuers must step away so the shock affects only the patient and does not injure anyone else nearby. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h6)

question: An AED has just been brought to the side of an adult patient in cardiac arrest. What is the very first thing the nurse should do with it?

options.A: Press the shock button
options.B: Apply the electrode pads
options.C: Check the battery level
options.D: Turn the AED on

explanation: Turning the device on activates the audio and visual prompts that guide the rest of the rescue steps. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid performing blind finger sweeps when clearing an airway obstruction?

options.A: It causes severe bleeding inside the oral cavity
options.B: It can push the foreign object deeper into the airway
options.C: It breaks the patient's lower teeth and gums
options.D: It triggers an irreversible spasm of the vocal cords

explanation: Blind finger sweeps risk jamming a loose object further down the throat, making the blockage worse. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h7)

question: Which of the following is a common physical complication of performing high-quality chest compressions?

options.A: Severe internal bleeding
options.B: Rupture of the liver
options.C: Puncture of both lungs
options.D: Rib or sternal fractures

explanation: Compressing the chest hard enough to circulate blood frequently causes fractured ribs, which is an accepted risk. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h7)

question: When is it appropriate for a nurse to stop performing CPR?

options.A: When trained medical help arrives and takes over care
options.B: When family members ask the team to take a break
options.C: As soon as the nurse feels physically tired and sweaty
options.D: After five minutes of continuous compressions without a pulse

explanation: CPR continues until the patient recovers, professionals take over, or clear signs of death appear. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h8)

question: Why is accurate timing and documentation following a cardiac arrest event so crucial?

options.A: It replaces the need for a verbal handover to the intensive care unit
options.B: It guarantees insurance payment for hospital equipment used
options.C: It is required only if the resuscitation attempt was completely successful
options.D: It provides a clear legal and clinical record of the emergency timeline

explanation: Detailed notes record the exact interventions and timing, which helps evaluate patient outcomes and guide future care. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T1#GNS212_U2_T1_h8)

question: What is the primary material used to construct the canopy of an oxygen tent?

options.A: Flexible silicone tubing
options.B: Woven cotton fabric
options.C: Clear plastic sheeting
options.D: Reinforced rubber mesh

explanation: Clear plastic is used so the healthcare team can continuously observe the patient's face, skin color, and respiratory effort without opening the enclosure. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why are oxygen tents more commonly utilized in pediatric wards rather than adult medical-surgical units?

options.A: Adults require higher flow rates than a tent mechanism can provide
options.B: Adult lungs are too large to benefit from canopy-delivered humidity
options.C: Pediatric patients have a lower metabolic demand for oxygen
options.D: Children are more accepting of a confined canopy than nasal prongs

explanation: Infants and toddlers frequently pull out nasal cannulas or fight facial masks, making an enclosed tent a practical way to deliver oxygen without constant physical resistance. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which respiratory condition in infants is a primary indication for the humidified environment of an oxygen tent?

options.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.B: Spontaneous pneumothorax
options.C: Acute bronchiolitis
options.D: Pulmonary embolism

explanation: Bronchiolitis causes inflammation and mucus plugging in the small airways of infants, making humidified oxygen delivery via a tent a valuable supportive therapy. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: What therapeutic property besides oxygenation makes the tent particularly beneficial for children suffering from croup?

options.A: Warming of inspired air to prevent systemic hypothermia
options.B: Direct delivery of nebulized systemic antibiotics
options.C: High moisture content that reduces upper airway swelling
options.D: Complete elimination of carbon dioxide from the airways

explanation: The cool, heavily humidified air inside the tent helps soothe irritated mucosal membranes and decreases the characteristic seal-like barking cough of croup. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the cooling mechanism built into an oxygen tent unit?

options.A: Freezing moisture to prevent water droplets from entering the patient's airway
options.B: Lowering the patient's core body temperature during a febrile episode
options.C: Preventing the interior from overheating due to body heat and trapped air
options.D: Cooling the oxygen tank to prevent structural expansion of the metal

explanation: Because the plastic canopy traps body heat and exhaled air, a refrigeration unit is necessary to keep the internal microclimate comfortable for the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why must high initial flow rates be used when first activating an oxygen tent?

options.A: To rapidly flush out carbon dioxide and achieve the prescribed oxygen concentration
options.B: To activate the internal cooling thermostat via rapid gas expansion
options.C: To dry out excess condensation accumulating inside the vinyl walls
options.D: To force the plastic canopy to inflate and create a rigid structural dome

explanation: Starting with a high flow rate clears out exhaled carbon dioxide that would otherwise accumulate inside the enclosed space and cause hypercapnia. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h3)

question: A nurse notices that condensation is heavily obscuring the plastic walls of an oxygen tent. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Increase the oxygen flow rate to maximum capacity to blow away droplets
options.B: Remove the child from the tent and switch immediately to a nasal cannula
options.C: Disconnect the oxygen source entirely until the moisture evaporates
options.D: Wipe down the interior or adjust the cooling and humidity controls

explanation: Heavy condensation blocks direct visual observation of the patient, requiring the nurse to clear the view and regulate the unit's temperature settings to balance humidity. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: Which parameter must be checked regularly inside the tent using a specialized analyzer tool?

options.A: Ambient room illumination
options.B: Relative humidity index
options.C: Barometric air pressure
options.D: Oxygen concentration percentage

explanation: Periodic measurement with an oxygen analyzer confirms that the delivered fraction of inspired oxygen matches the clinical prescription, as leaks in the canopy can dilute the gas mixture. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h4)

question: Which lubricant type should a nurse select when a patient inside an oxygen tent requires lip hydration?

options.A: Synthetic liquid paraffin
options.B: Water-soluble jelly
options.C: Petroleum-based ointment
options.D: Mineral oil extract

explanation: Petroleum-based products are highly flammable in oxygen-enriched environments and must be replaced with water-soluble alternatives to prevent facial burns. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why are battery-operated electronic toys strictly prohibited inside or immediately next to an oxygen tent?

options.A: Plastic components from the toys will melt from the high oxygen concentration
options.B: Small electrical sparks from switches or motors can ignite the oxygen-rich air
options.C: The noise generated prevents accurate auscultation of breath sounds
options.D: Electromagnetic fields interfere with the humidifier's cooling thermostat

explanation: Any micro-spark from a mechanical switch or failing battery contact can instantly trigger a fire in the presence of concentrated oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h5)

question: What happens to the internal oxygen concentration every time the tent canopy is unzipped or lifted wide open?

options.A: It converts temporarily into carbon dioxide gas pockets
options.B: It remains completely stable if the flowmeter is left running
options.C: It drops rapidly due to mixing with room air
options.D: It spikes dangerously due to ambient pressure compression

explanation: Opening the canopy breaks the sealed environment, allowing room air to flood the space and dilute the therapeutic oxygen concentration. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is a primary risk to an infant's thermal regulation when housed inside a refrigerated oxygen tent?

options.A: Hypothermia from cold circulating air and damp clothing
options.B: Heat stroke caused by direct sunlight exposure
options.C: Severe dehydration from excessive skin evaporation
options.D: Hyperthermia from trapped body heat and failed cooling fans

explanation: The combination of the refrigeration unit's cooling action and wet garments from humidity can quickly lower an infant's core body temperature. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T10#GNS212_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the main goal of giving oxygen therapy with a face mask?

options.A: Permanently cure chronic respiratory diseases
options.B: Lower the patient's baseline body temperature
options.C: Maintain safe arterial oxygen saturation levels
options.D: Increase the patient's total body weight

explanation: You give extra oxygen mainly to keep the patient's blood oxygen in a safe range and stop their tissues from lacking air. You've got this!

question: When would you choose a face mask instead of a nasal cannula for oxygen delivery?

options.A: When the patient only requires a very low flow rate of oxygen
options.B: When the patient refuses to have anything touching their face
options.C: When the patient is completely free of any respiratory distress
options.D: When the patient needs higher and more precise oxygen concentrations

explanation: Face masks cover both the nose and mouth, making them the go-to choice when a patient in distress needs a stronger, concentrated flow of oxygen.

question: Why is a Venturi mask often chosen for patients with COPD?

options.A: It pumps high-pressure air directly into the stomach.
options.B: It allows the patient to eat and drink without removing it.
options.C: It delivers a precise and controlled concentration of oxygen.
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any humidification.

explanation: Venturi masks use clever color-coded adapters to give an exact percentage of oxygen, keeping vulnerable COPD patients safe.

question: What is the purpose of attaching a humidifier bottle filled with sterile water to the oxygen setup?

options.A: Add pleasant artificial fragrances to the oxygen flow
options.B: Moisten dry medical gas to prevent mucous membrane irritation
options.C: Filter out all bacteria from the room air
options.D: Measure the exact blood pressure of the patient

explanation: Medical oxygen is very dry. Adding moisture protects the delicate lining of your patient's nose and throat from drying out and cracking.

question: Which piece of equipment do you need to safely connect an oxygen mask to a hospital wall supply?

options.A: Sphygmomanometer
options.B: Suction canister
options.C: Flowmeter
options.D: Glucometer strip

explanation: The flowmeter plugs into the wall outlet so you can easily control and measure the liters per minute flowing to the patient.

question: What is a major safety rule you must enforce when a patient is receiving oxygen therapy?

options.A: Keep all open flames and smoking materials away from the area
options.B: Remove all metal objects from the entire hospital floor
options.C: Turn off all room lights to keep the oxygen cool
options.D: Keep the patient lying completely flat on their back at all times

explanation: Oxygen makes fires catch faster and burn much hotter! Always make sure sparks, matches, and cigarettes stay far away.

question: You are about to put an oxygen mask on an anxious patient. What is your best first nursing action?

options.A: Explain the procedure simply to reduce anxiety and calm the patient
options.B: Tie the mask straps as tightly as possible to prevent removal
options.C: Leave the room immediately and let the patient put the mask on alone
options.D: Administer a strong sedative drug without a doctor's order

explanation: Talking calmly to your patient builds trust, eases their panic, and helps them breathe much easier during the setup.

question: Why should you mold the metal strip of a face mask over the patient's nose bridge?

options.A: To increase the structural weight of the plastic device
options.B: To stop the patient from speaking to the nursing staff
options.C: To lock the patient's jaw in a closed position during sleep
options.D: To prevent oxygen from leaking upward into the patient's eyes

explanation: Molding the nose piece stops air from blowing into the eyes and drying them out, while ensuring the patient gets their full dose.

question: How often should you check the skin where an oxygen mask and its straps rest?

options.A: Only when the patient complains of severe bleeding
options.B: Regularly during routine shifts and care checks
options.C: Only once a week before the patient is discharged
options.D: Never, because oxygen masks do not touch the skin

explanation: Checking the skin often helps you catch early redness and prevents pressure sores from the plastic edges and elastic bands.

question: A patient on face mask oxygen suddenly drops in saturation and the tubing feels warm and static. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Normal adjustment of the lungs to high flow rates
options.B: A kink or blockage in the oxygen delivery tubing
options.C: The humidifier bottle being completely overfilled
options.D: An increase in the patient's physical activity level

explanation: If the tubing gets twisted or blocked, the oxygen stops flowing, causing saturation levels to drop fast. Always check the lines first!

question: What is a major danger of giving high-flow oxygen to a patient who retains carbon dioxide?

options.A: Rapid increase in the patient's daily fluid retention
options.B: Loss of the hypoxic drive, leading to respiratory depression
options.C: Sudden development of severe skin allergies on the face
options.D: Permanent discoloration of the nose and cheek tissues

explanation: Some chronic lung patients breathe because their oxygen is low. Giving too much oxygen can make their brain say 'we don't need to breathe anymore,' which is dangerous.

question: Which nursing action helps prevent skin breakdown caused by oxygen mask straps?

options.A: Apply strong medical adhesive tape directly to the forehead
options.B: Remove the mask permanently and stop all oxygen therapy
options.C: Place protective padding under pressure points and check skin often
options.D: Pull the elastic straps tighter so the mask never shifts

explanation: Padding shares the load evenly across the skin, and checking frequently lets you spot irritation before it turns into a wound.

question: What is the primary purpose of tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: Removal of accumulated lower airway secretions
options.B: Delivery of high-flow humidified oxygen
options.C: Measurement of central venous pressure
options.D: Expansion of collapsed alveolar sacs

explanation: Suctioning clears mucus, blood, and debris that the patient cannot expel due to an artificial airway or impaired cough reflex. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do patients with artificial airways require routine suctioning?

options.A: Endotracheal tubes actively secrete excess mucus into the lungs
options.B: Upper airway defenses are permanently destroyed by intubation
options.C: Artificial airways bypass normal upper airway filtration and impair coughing
options.D: Mechanical ventilators force fluid into the lower respiratory tract

explanation: Bypassing the upper airway stops natural conditioning of inspired air, leading to thicker secretions and an ineffective cough mechanism. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: When is the most appropriate time to perform tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: Every two hours strictly according to the standard hospital shift schedule
options.B: Immediately before every routine repositioning maneuver
options.C: Whenever the patient expresses mild anxiety about breathing
options.D: Only when clinical indicators like adventitious sounds or desaturation appear

explanation: Routine scheduled suctioning causes unnecessary mucosal trauma and hypoxemia without clinical benefit; it must be done PRN based on assessment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which physical finding is a primary indication for airway suctioning?

options.A: Coarse crackles or rhonchi heard over the large airways
options.B: Asymmetrical chest expansion during quiet breathing
options.C: Muffled heart sounds and distant peripheral pulses
options.D: Decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes

explanation: Audible or auscultated secretions in the airway indicate that mucus has accumulated and requires mechanical removal. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the recommended safe range of negative pressure for suctioning an adult patient?

options.A: 40 to 60 mmHg
options.B: 150 to 200 mmHg
options.C: 220 to 250 mmHg
options.D: 100 to 120 mmHg

explanation: Keeping negative pressure between 100 and 120 mmHg for adults effectively removes secretions while minimizing trauma to delicate tracheal mucosa. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: How should the correct size of a suction catheter be determined relative to the artificial airway?

options.A: It should be twice as wide as the tracheostomy opening to clear walls
options.B: Its outer diameter should not exceed half the internal diameter of the airway
options.C: It must match the exact internal diameter of the endotracheal tube
options.D: Size selection is arbitrary as long as the catheter fits through the adapter

explanation: A catheter that is too large occludes the airway entirely, trapping air and causing severe negative pressure trauma and rapid de-recruitment of alveoli. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: Why is hyperoxygenation performed immediately before tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: To flush out residual carbon dioxide trapped in the ventilator tubing
options.B: To offset the temporary removal of oxygen from the lungs during suctioning
options.C: To stimulate the cough reflex and mobilize trapped lower airway secretions
options.D: To liquefy thick mucus plugs located deep in the smaller bronchioles

explanation: Suction catheters withdraw air and oxygen from the airway, so pre-oxygenating builds a reserve to prevent dangerous drops in blood oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the standard duration for pre-oxygenating an adult patient prior to suctioning?

options.A: 2 to 3 minutes
options.B: 5 to 10 minutes
options.C: 30 to 60 seconds
options.D: Exactly 15 seconds

explanation: Providing 100% oxygen for 30 to 60 seconds safely elevates blood oxygen saturation prior to introducing the catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the maximum recommended duration for a single suctioning pass?

options.A: 10 to 15 seconds
options.B: 1 to 2 minutes
options.C: 30 to 45 seconds
options.D: 5 seconds maximum

explanation: Limiting each pass to 10 to 15 seconds prevents excessive oxygen loss and minimizes the risk of cardiac arrhythmias caused by hypoxia. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: A nurse is inserting a suction catheter into an endotracheal tube. At what point should negative pressure be applied?

options.A: Before entering the tube to suck away upper airway secretions
options.B: Only when the catheter hits resistance at the mainstem bronchus
options.C: Only while withdrawing the catheter with a rotating motion
options.D: Continuously during both insertion and withdrawal phases

explanation: Applying suction during insertion damages the fragile tracheal mucosa and increases oxygen depletion; suction is strictly applied on withdrawal. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if a patient develops severe bradycardia or irregular heart rhythms during suctioning?

options.A: Increase the vacuum pressure to clear remaining mucus faster
options.B: Stop suctioning immediately and administer 100% oxygen
options.C: Administer an intravenous diuretic to reduce heart strain
options.D: Continue suctioning quickly to finish the pass before resting

explanation: Arrhythmias during suctioning usually stem from hypoxia or vagal stimulation; stopping and providing oxygen immediately reverses the trigger. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which complication is directly caused by applying suction pressure during catheter insertion?

options.A: Permanent paralysis of the vocal cords
options.B: Spontaneous collapse of the left ventricle
options.C: Trauma and bleeding of the tracheal mucosa
options.D: Severe systemic blood pressure elevation

explanation: Sucking while the catheter advances pulls the delicate mucosal lining against the suction eyelets, causing abrasion and hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to include when documenting a tracheobronchial suctioning procedure?

options.A: The color, consistency, and amount of secretions removed
options.B: The room temperature at the time of the intervention
options.C: The name of the manufacturer of the wall vacuum regulator
options.D: The exact brand name of the suction catheter used

explanation: Documenting secretion characteristics helps the healthcare team monitor for respiratory infection, hydration status, and disease progression. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: How does a nurse confirm that tracheobronchial suctioning was successful?

options.A: By ensuring the mechanical ventilator alarm stays silent for ten minutes
options.B: By checking that the patient has fallen into a deep, quiet sleep
options.C: By verifying that the suction canister is completely full of fluid
options.D: By noting improved breath sounds, stable vitals, and clear oxygen saturation

explanation: Success is determined by clinical indicators showing resolved airway obstruction, such as improved breath sounds and normalized oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the main job of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) during a cardiac arrest?

options.A: Provide mechanical chest compressions at a steady rate
options.B: Pump oxygen directly into the lungs of the patient
options.C: Measure the exact blood pressure of an unresponsive person
options.D: Deliver an electrical shock to reset an abnormal heart rhythm

explanation: Think of an AED as a smart device that checks the heart rhythm and gives a quick shock only when needed to get the heart beating right again. You've got this!

question: Why is using an AED as quickly as possible so important during cardiac arrest?

options.A: It automatically contacts the local police department for help
options.B: It permanently cures any underlying heart disease causing the arrest
options.C: It replaces the need to ever perform chest compressions
options.D: Survival rates drop significantly with every minute that defibrillation is delayed

explanation: Every single minute counts! Without blood flow, the brain quickly loses oxygen, so acting fast truly saves lives.

question: Which patient sign means you should grab and attach an AED right away?

options.A: Severe chest pain and heavy sweating
options.B: Confusion and mild shortness of breath
options.C: High fever and a rapid pulse rate
options.D: Unresponsiveness and no normal breathing

explanation: An AED is meant for sudden cardiac arrest. We look for someone who has collapsed, doesn't respond, and isn't breathing normally.

question: What happens if an AED is accidentally used on someone whose heart is beating normally?

options.A: The heart will instantly stop due to the excess electrical current
options.B: The device will analyze the rhythm and refuse to deliver a shock
options.C: The machine will automatically start delivering CPR compressions
options.D: The internal battery of the device will permanently burn out

explanation: Don't worry, AEDs are very smart! They scan the heart first and will block any shock if the heart rhythm is normal. They won't harm a healthy beat.

question: What is the job of the sticky adhesive pads that come with an AED?

options.A: Secure the patient firmly to the flat floor surface
options.B: Deliver a continuous supply of medical oxygen to the lungs
options.C: Transmit electrical current from the machine to the patient's heart
options.D: Measure the exact body temperature of the victim

explanation: The pads act as the bridge. They stick to the skin to read the heart rhythm and deliver the life-saving shock safely.

question: Why should you regularly check the status indicator light on an AED machine?

options.A: To calibrate the internal thermometer for accurate skin readings
options.B: To measure how many shocks are left in the main computer processor
options.C: To ensure the voice volume is loud enough for a noisy room
options.D: To confirm that the internal battery and system components are operational

explanation: Routine checks make sure the machine is ready to work the exact second an emergency happens. Good nursing practice!

question: Where should you place the two AED pads on an adult patient's bare chest?

options.A: Center of the chest and middle of the back
options.B: Left side of the ribs and right side of the abdomen
options.C: Both shoulders near the neck collarbones
options.D: Upper right chest and lower left ribcage

explanation: Placing one pad on the upper right and the other on the lower left lets the electrical current flow diagonally right through the heart muscle.

question: What is the very next thing you must do after the AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Check the carotid pulse for at least one full minute
options.B: Turn the machine off and wait for the ambulance crew
options.C: Remove the sticky pads and wipe the skin with alcohol
options.D: Resume chest compressions and CPR for two minutes

explanation: Right after a shock, don't wait—jump right back into CPR starting with chest compressions to keep blood moving!

question: How should you handle an implanted pacemaker lump when placing an AED pad?

options.A: Refuse to use the AED because pacemakers block all shocks
options.B: Place the pad at least one inch away from the device lump
options.C: Place the pad directly over the lump to boost the shock
options.D: Cut out the pacemaker wires before attaching the sticky pads

explanation: Keep the pad about an inch away from a pacemaker lump so the machine's energy goes into the heart instead of damaging the device.

question: What safety step is required if a patient experiencing cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of water?

options.A: Turn off all nearby electrical appliances in the room
options.B: Double the number of chest compressions you deliver
options.C: Move the patient to a dry area and dry the chest
options.D: Place rubber mats under your own shoes while working

explanation: Water conducts electricity. Moving the patient to dry ground and wiping their chest ensures the shock goes through the heart, not out into the water.

question: What usually causes an AED to flash a 'Check Pads' error message?

options.A: The patient's heart rate is too fast for the machine to read
options.B: The rescuer is pressing the shock button at the wrong time
options.C: Loose cable connections or moisture on the patient's skin
options.D: The battery inside the computer unit is completely dead

explanation: If pads aren't sticking well or the skin is wet, the machine can't get a good connection. A quick dry and press usually fixes it!

question: What must you do immediately when the AED announces 'Movement Detected'?

options.A: Shake the patient harder to restart the heart rhythm
options.B: Unplug the machine and replace both electrode pads
options.C: Stop chest compressions and ensure everyone steps back
options.D: Increase the speed of rescue breaths being delivered

explanation: Movement—even from CPR—can trick the AED into reading the wrong thing. Always step back and stay clear while it analyzes.

question: What should you do with the AED pads if the patient suddenly wakes up and starts breathing?

options.A: Move both pads to the patient's back to keep the skin warm
options.B: Peel them off immediately and throw them in the trash
options.C: Leave the pads attached to the chest in case arrest recurs
options.D: Wipe them down with bleach and pack them in the box

explanation: Leave the pads on! A recovered patient can still slip back into cardiac arrest very quickly, and you want the AED ready to go.

question: Why is placing an unconscious, breathing patient into the recovery position so important?

options.A: It keeps the airway clear and prevents aspiration of fluids
options.B: It stops involuntary muscle spasms in the arms and legs
options.C: It makes it easier to reapply the AED pads if needed
options.D: It lowers the patient's elevated blood pressure quickly

explanation: The recovery position uses gravity to keep the tongue and saliva from blocking the airway of someone who is knocked out. Safety first!

question: What is the main goal of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)?

options.A: To calculate the correct medication dosage for the child
options.B: To perform a rapid, hands-off visual evaluation from the doorway
options.C: To measure the exact blood pressure and temperature
options.D: To listen carefully to heart murmurs with a stethoscope

explanation: You don't even need to touch the child right away! The PAT is a quick, visual tool you can use from the doorway to size up how sick a little one is.

question: A child comes in with chest retractions, nasal flaring, and breathing very fast. Which part of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle does this show?

options.A: Circulation to the skin
options.B: Work of breathing
options.C: Appearance
options.D: Neurological status

explanation: Spotting retractions and nasal flaring tells you right away how hard the child is working to pull air in. That's all about their work of breathing!

question: Why is a slow heart rate (bradycardia) in a sick baby or child such a red flag?

options.A: It is a normal response to mild fever
options.B: It means the heart muscle is exceptionally strong
options.C: It proves the child is well-conditioned
options.D: It usually indicates impending cardiac arrest

explanation: Unlike adults who might have a slow heart rate because they are fit athletes, sick kids drop their heart rate when their body is failing and running out of oxygen. It's a serious warning sign!

question: What makes an infant's upper airway much easier to block compared to an adult's?

options.A: A larger tongue relative to the oral cavity
options.B: A much wider trachea and larynx
options.C: Complete rigidity of the upper airway cartilage
options.D: An absence of mucus glands in the pharynx

explanation: Babies have surprisingly large tongues for their little mouths! If their head isn't positioned quite right, that tongue can easily slide back and block their airway.

question: When two rescuers are doing CPR on a child, what is the compression-to-ventilation ratio?

options.A: 5 compressions to 1 breath
options.B: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
options.C: 100 compressions to 5 breaths
options.D: 15 compressions to 2 breaths

explanation: When you have two people working together on a pediatric patient, you use a 15:2 ratio to get more rescue breaths into the child.

question: Why is letting the chest spring all the way back up between compressions so important during CPR?

options.A: It gives the rescuer time to rest their arms
options.B: It lowers the child's body temperature
options.C: It prevents the ribs from fracturing
options.D: It allows blood to refill the heart chambers

explanation: Think of the heart like a sponge. When you push down, you squeeze blood out; when you let the chest recoil, it refills with fresh blood for the next push!

question: What is a major danger of giving a child too many breaths during resuscitation?

options.A: Causing immediate permanent brain damage from too much oxygen
options.B: Lowering the child's heart rate into normal ranges
options.C: Preventing the lungs from ever collapsing
options.D: Increasing intrathoracic pressure and reducing blood return to the heart

explanation: If you bag a child too fast or too hard, you trap too much pressure inside their chest. That extra pressure actually blocks blood from flowing back to the heart.

question: Why should you avoid tilting an infant's head too far back when opening their airway?

options.A: It completely stops spontaneous breathing
options.B: It always causes immediate cervical spine fractures
options.C: The flexible trachea can kink and cause an obstruction
options.D: It makes it impossible to check the pulse

explanation: An infant's windpipe is soft and flexible. If you tilt their head back too far (hyperextension), the airway actually kinks shut like a bent garden hose!

question: Which sign tells you that a child's breathing problem is getting worse and turning into respiratory failure?

options.A: Slow, irregular breathing and cyanosis
options.B: An increase in spontaneous talking
options.C: Loud, powerful crying and high energy
options.D: Rapid, deep breathing with normal skin color

explanation: At first, a struggling child breathes super fast. But once their muscles get too tired, they slow down, breathe irregularly, and turn blue (cyanosis). That's a true emergency!

question: A toddler arrives at the emergency unit suddenly drooling, making high-pitched breathing sounds (stridor), and very restless, but has no cough. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep the child calm and avoid invasive examinations
options.B: Immediately force the child to lie flat for an X-ray
options.C: Attempt to visualize the vocal cords with a tongue depressor
options.D: Administer oral fluids immediately to soothe the throat

explanation: This sounds like epiglottitis! If you upset or cry the child, their swollen airway can snap shut completely. Keep them calm in their mother's arms and don't force anything into their mouth.

question: If a seriously ill child has a completely normal blood pressure reading, does that mean they are out of danger?

options.A: Fluid resuscitation is definitely not needed
options.B: The child is completely free from danger
options.C: Cardiac output is at its absolute maximum
options.D: The child may still be in compensated shock

explanation: Kids are amazing at squeezing their blood vessels tight to keep their blood pressure looking normal, even when they are crashing. A normal BP doesn't mean they aren't in shock!

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard type of shock seen in children?

options.A: Cardiogenic shock
options.B: Distributive shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Metabolic shock

explanation: You'll hear about hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive shock in pediatrics—'metabolic shock' isn't one of the classic categories.

question: What is the most common heart rhythm seen when a child goes into cardiac arrest?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation with rapid response
options.B: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia
options.C: Ventricular fibrillation
options.D: Asystole or pulseless electrical activity

explanation: Unlike adults who often arrest with a shockable rhythm like VF, children usually arrest after a long period of low oxygen, leading straight to asystole or PEA.

question: During a pediatric resuscitation, how often should epinephrine be given?

options.A: Only after five defibrillation shocks
options.B: Every 3 to 5 minutes
options.C: Once every hour
options.D: Every 30 seconds

explanation: Epinephrine is a trusty emergency medication given every 3 to 5 minutes during a code to help keep blood flowing to the heart and brain.

question: What is a major focus of care right after a child's heartbeat and breathing return (after ROSC)?

options.A: Discontinuing all cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.B: Minimizing secondary brain injury and multi-organ damage
options.C: Withholding all fluids to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Allowing the child's body temperature to rise unchecked

explanation: Getting their pulse back is a huge win, but the job isn't done! Now we have to protect their organs—especially the brain—from further stress and damage.

question: Why is developing a fever especially dangerous for a child right after they recover from cardiac arrest?

options.A: It stops all medications from working
options.B: It automatically triggers another cardiac arrest
options.C: It increases the metabolic demand of the injured brain
options.D: It proves the resuscitation attempt failed entirely

explanation: When a child's brain is recovering from lack of oxygen, a fever forces it to work much harder and use up oxygen it simply doesn't have to spare.

question: Where does the actual exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide take place in the lungs?

options.A: Within the upper pharynx
options.B: Inside the main trachea
options.C: In the tiny alveoli
options.D: Through the vocal cords

explanation: Alveoli are surrounded by tiny blood vessels where oxygen and carbon dioxide easily pass back and forth. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: What happens inside the chest cavity when the diaphragm muscle contracts during inhalation?

options.A: Chest volume increases and air is pulled inward
options.B: The lungs collapse due to increased internal pressure
options.C: Chest volume decreases and air is pushed outward
options.D: Air pressure inside the lungs becomes higher than outside

explanation: Contracting the diaphragm flattens it out, making the chest cavity bigger and creating a vacuum that draws air into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: What is the normal resting breathing rate for a healthy adult in breaths per minute?

options.A: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.B: 25 to 35 breaths per minute
options.C: 5 to 10 breaths per minute
options.D: 40 to 50 breaths per minute

explanation: A healthy adult at rest normally breathes between 12 and 20 times every minute. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: A patient is using their neck and shoulder muscles heavily to take every breath. What does this sign indicate?

options.A: The patient has a normal, healthy breathing pattern
options.B: The patient's lungs are expanding with minimal effort
options.C: The patient is in a deeply relaxed sleeping state
options.D: The patient is experiencing increased respiratory effort and distress

explanation: Using accessory muscles means the main breathing muscles need extra help because breathing has become difficult. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why might a patient with low oxygen levels first appear restless and confused?

options.A: Restlessness is a side effect of normal breathing
options.B: The patient's stomach is empty during the assessment
options.C: The patient is reacting to cold hospital room temperatures
options.D: The brain is sensitive to a shortage of oxygen

explanation: Brain tissue needs a constant, heavy supply of oxygen, so even mild shortages quickly cause mental changes like confusion or anxiety. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following is considered a late sign of low oxygen levels in the body?

options.A: Mild restlessness and anxiety
options.B: Leaning forward in a tripod position
options.C: Cyanosis or bluish skin discoloration
options.D: An increased breathing rate

explanation: Skin turning blue usually happens only after oxygen levels have dropped severely for some time. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which bed position is best for instantly helping an out-of-breath patient expand their lungs?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: High-Fowler's position
options.C: Prone lying position
options.D: Flat supine position

explanation: Sitting upright in High-Fowler's position uses gravity to push abdominal organs downward, giving the lungs more room to fill with air. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: A patient with thick mucus cannot clear their throat and shows signs of airway blockage. What immediate nursing action is required?

options.A: Asking the patient to hold their breath for one minute
options.B: Placing the patient flat on their back to rest
options.C: Suctioning the airway to remove the trapped secretions
options.D: Administering a dose of blood pressure medication

explanation: When a patient cannot cough up mucus blocking their airway, suctioning physically clears the passage so air can flow. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which oxygen delivery device is best for providing an exact, controlled percentage of oxygen to a patient?

options.A: Non-rebreather bag
options.B: Standard nasal cannula
options.C: Venturi mask
options.D: Simple face mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses special adapter barrels to mix room air and oxygen precisely, delivering a specific, reliable oxygen percentage. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why must petroleum jelly and open flames be strictly avoided around active oxygen delivery equipment?

options.A: Grease stops the oxygen machine from making a buzzing sound
options.B: Oxygen strongly supports and quickens combustion and fire
options.C: Petroleum products block the tiny holes in the nasal cannula
options.D: Flames cause the oxygen tank to instantly fill with water

explanation: Oxygen makes fires burn much hotter and faster, so any spark or flame near an oxygen source creates an extreme fire hazard. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of pursed-lip breathing for a patient with chronic breathing difficulties?

options.A: It stops the heart from beating too fast during movement
options.B: It keeps airways open longer by creating gentle back-pressure during exhalation
options.C: It forces all the air out of the lungs in a single quick second
options.D: It pumps extra water vapor directly into the stomach lining

explanation: Breathing out through pursed lips creates small back-pressure that stops fragile airways from collapsing too early during exhalation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of having a surgical patient use an incentive spirometer?

options.A: To pump liquid medicine directly into the throat
options.B: To check the patient's blood pressure levels
options.C: To measure how loudly the patient can talk
options.D: To encourage deep breathing and prevent lung collapse

explanation: Incentive spirometry makes patients take deep, deliberate breaths, keeping their alveoli open and preventing postoperative atelectasis. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which factor can cause a pulse oximeter sensor to give an inaccurate reading on a patient's finger?

options.A: Cold fingers and poor peripheral circulation
options.B: Speaking in a normal tone of voice during the test
options.C: Drinking a glass of cold water before testing
options.D: A high room temperature on the hospital ward

explanation: Pulse oximeters rely on good blood flow through the finger; if circulation is sluggish or cold, the machine cannot read the pulse well. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which nursing action helps thin thick respiratory secretions so they are easier for the patient to cough up?

options.A: Lying the patient flat on their back
options.B: Keeping the room air completely dry
options.C: Encouraging adequate daily fluid intake
options.D: Restricting all drinking water after meals

explanation: Drinking enough water keeps body fluids thin, which naturally loosens thick mucus in the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of inhalation therapy?

options.A: To deliver medication directly to the respiratory tract
options.B: To remove excess fluid directly from the pleural space
options.C: To bypass the digestive system completely for nutrition
options.D: To increase blood pressure through systemic absorption

explanation: Inhalation therapy deposits drugs straight into the airways and lungs for a localized effect. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is inhalation therapy often preferred over oral medications for lung conditions?

options.A: It guarantees 100 percent absorption into the bloodstream
options.B: It works faster locally and reduces widespread side effects
options.C: It is completely free of any potential complications
options.D: It never requires patient coordination or special training

explanation: Targeting the lungs directly means smaller doses can treat the problem without affecting the rest of the body as heavily. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which part of the respiratory tract filters out large particles before they reach the lungs?

options.A: The upper airway and nose
options.B: The pulmonary alveoli
options.C: The terminal bronchioles
options.D: The visceral pleura

explanation: The nasal passages and upper airway warm, humidify, and filter incoming air, catching larger debris and particles. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: What particle size is generally needed for medication to reach the deep lower airways and alveoli?

options.A: Between 50 and 100 micrometers
options.B: Greater than 20 micrometers
options.C: Between 1 and 5 micrometers
options.D: Any visible dust particle size

explanation: Fine particles measuring 1 to 5 micrometers are small enough to bypass the upper airway and settle deep in the bronchioles and alveoli. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which inhalation device requires the patient to take a fast, forceful breath to activate medication delivery?

options.A: Dry Powder Inhaler
options.B: Metered-dose inhaler with spacer
options.C: Simple nasal cannula
options.D: Standard nebulizer machine

explanation: Dry Powder Inhalers rely entirely on the patient's own inhalation effort to pull the powder out of the device and into the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: When is a nebulizer most commonly chosen over a metered-dose inhaler?

options.A: When the patient needs a device that fits easily in a small shirt pocket
options.B: When treatment must be completed in less than five seconds
options.C: When the patient cannot coordinate deep breathing with a handheld inhaler
options.D: When the healthcare provider wants to avoid using any electricity or gas

explanation: Nebulizers produce a continuous mist over several minutes, making them great for young children, the elderly, or acutely breathless patients. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary condition treated using emergency inhaled bronchodilators?

options.A: Acute bronchospasm
options.B: Lower extremity deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Chronic bacterial skin infection
options.D: Severe iron-deficiency anemia
